items.subject: The MAGA World Incentives That Have Saved Max Miller
bullets: IT IS NO SECRET that President Trump has built his “alpha male” persona around a warped version of masculinity in which vulnerability is weakness, cruelty is strength, empathy is feminine, and women are easy targets. It’s also no secret tha…

Over the past decade, Republican politics has become obsessed with projecting toughness and mocking liberals as weak, feminine “betas.” Beneath it all is a deep disdain for women. In Trump’s case specifically, it wasn’t even all that hidden…

items.subject: ICYMI: Mehdi’s No-Holds-Barred Sit-Down With Hunter Biden
bullets: Hunter Biden claims his father enabled Israel’s Gaza campaign and praised Netanyahu, while revealing his own addiction struggles and alleged role in the “Biden crime family” narrative.

items.subject: Trump Took His Status. ICE Took His Dignity. He Took His Life.
bullets: In July 2024, a Supreme Court ruling allowed the Trump administration to end Temporary Protected Status for 350,000 Haitians, leading to Pierre Bel’s ankle‑monitoring and eventual death after a tractor‑trail collision.

Pierre, a Haitian TPS recipient, was denied a soccer scholarship at Wittenberg, forced to enroll at Wright State, and faced bullying and humiliation while wearing an ankle monitor, which he claimed was withheld from his JROTC uniform.

Haitian community leaders and faith figures blamed the Trump‑era deportation policy for Pierre’s death, calling for an end to ankle‑monitor shackling and highlighting the historical parallels to Haiti’s 1915 U.S. occupation and ongoing human‑rights abuses.

items.subject: John Roberts Sounded the Alarm on Trump’s Illegal Ballroom (w/ George Conway)
bullets: Robinson and Conway warn that Trump’s push to restrict mail‑in voting before the midterms could backfire if the chaotic USPS reforms are ultimately struck down by the Supreme Court.
They note SCOTUS has allowed Trump’s controversial ballroom construction to proceed, but Democrats may move to halt it in January, while Epstein‑related questions remain under‑reported.

items.subject: Will Republicans Be Asked to Disavow Elon Musk Over His Latest Creepy Antisemitic Post?
bullets: Elon Musk sparked outrage by posting a poll questioning Jewish racial identity and suggesting DNA proof is needed, echoing historic antisemitic tropes and prompting criticism from the ADL and commentators.

Musk, the GOP’s top donor, has pledged at least $100 million for mid‑term races and recently disclosed $800,000 in spending, raising questions whether Republican candidates will be pressured to denounce his antisemitic remarks.
The newsletter contrasts this with Democrats’ demand that left‑leaning streamer Hasan Piker disavow alleged antisemitism, highlighting a double standard in political accountability.

items.subject: Ingots We No Longer Trust
bullets: Krugman likens central‑bank gold reserves to Yap’s massive stone money, noting that most gold sits in the New York Fed and changes hands without moving the metal.

He warns that the Trump administration’s disregard for rule of law makes a seizure of that gold plausible, prompting the Dutch (shifting $12 bn) and French central banks to relocate gold to London and Paris.
While the moves have negligible financial impact, they signal a loss of trust in the U.S. to honor international agreements, a reputation that will take years to rebuild.

items.subject: Ted Cruz’s New Biography of Clarence Thomas Is About Becoming a Supreme Court Justice – Himself
bullets: Ted Cruz’s new book, *Going Further: The Incomparable Clarence Thomas*, is a hagiographic biography that highlights Cruz’s past Supreme Court cases and his own legal views rather than outlining his potential judicial philosophy.
Cruz tells NPR’s Steve Inskeep he would never become a judge because judges stay out of politics, yet the author notes that Supreme Court justices, including Thomas, are deeply political actors.
The piece criticizes Cruz’s claim as disingenuous, suggesting the biography serves more as a personal promotion ahead of the presidential election than a serious legal study.

items.subject: Europe’s Gold Fled the Nazis. Now It’s Fleeing Trump.
bullets: Dutch central bank moved $12 billion of gold from New York to London vaults, citing concerns over Trump’s policies; France followed by selling $15 billion of New York bullion and storing it in Paris.
Germany and Italy, the U.S.’s second and third largest gold holders, are debating pulling their reserves from U.S. vaults, reflecting a growing distrust of American leadership under Trump.

items.subject: Inside Trump’s Nightmare for Haitians in Springfield: ‘We’re Following Our Orders’
bullets: Trump’s administration dismantled Haitian Temporary Protected Status and used ICE to launch a sweeping crackdown in Springfield, Ohio, targeting the local Haitian community after years of racist rhetoric
The Supreme Court’s right‑wing supermajority upheld the crackdown, which immigration lawyer Katie Kersh says is a test case for broader, nationwide anti‑immigrant enforcement
The campaign has created pervasive fear, with residents fearing to leave their homes as the government enforces a militarized ‘law and order’ agenda against a vulnerable minority

items.subject: Pennsylvania Republicans: We’re Toast
bullets: GOP nominee for Pennsylvania governor Stacy Garrity trails incumbent Josh Shapiro by 16‑31 points in recent polls and faces a ten‑to‑one fundraising gap, with Shapiro ahead by $16 million.

Republican leaders including Rep. Mike Kelly and Rep. Dan Meuser describe Garrity’s race as an uphill battle, noting Shapiro’s strong war chest, incumbency advantage, and even some cautious GOP support for the Democrat.
In Florida’s 7th District, GOP candidate Ryan Elijah faces an ethics complaint for failing to disclose the sources of up to $5.1 million in personal assets, a violation of House disclosure rules.

items.subject: Chevron: A Deep Dive
bullets: Doomberg released an 80‑minute deep‑dive on Chevron, covering supermajor dynamics, Chevron’s global asset mix, key growth opportunities, and investment considerations.
For the next two weeks, new subscribers—both $400/year and $1200/year tiers—receive free full access to the Chevron presentation, plus the archive of 500+ articles, before the offer ends Sept 18.

items.subject: Pete Hegseth Is a F*cking Moron. And We’re Paying for It.
bullets: Sen. Thom Tillis urged President Trump to fire Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, citing his incompetence and focus on culture wars over national defense.

Hegseth mocked a Canadian cadet photo on Twitter, misrepresenting Canadian soldiers and undermining U.S.-Canada military cooperation, while 158 Canadian Armed Forces members died in Afghanistan fighting alongside the U.S.

items.subject: The Murder-for-Hire Plot Rocking MAGA Land
bullets: Fernando Cerimedo, dubbed “MAGA’s Man in Latin America,” once a driver‑for‑hire and alleged real estate fraudster, advised right‑wing leaders like Argentina’s Javier Milei and Honduras’s Nasry Asfura while earning a “Hispanic Political Consultant of the Year” award at Mar‑a‑Lago in February 2024.
During the gala, Cerimedo publicly thanked former Trump campaign tech chief Brad Parscale for believing in him and providing technology, highlighting his close ties to the Trump orbit.

On August 17, hitmen in Bolivia attempted to murder Cerimedo’s pregnant ex‑girlfriend Nadia Beller, who survived and began revealing details that could implicate Cerimedo in the attack and expose broader Trump‑linked operations in Latin America.

items.subject: Here’s How You Tax the Billionaires
bullets: Gabriel Zucman argues that a wealth tax targeting assets, not income, is needed because billionaires like Musk and Bezos often report zero income and avoid taxes through holding companies.
He defends wealth taxes against claims they deter investment, citing California’s Proposition 40 (a one‑time 5% tax on state billionaires) and the UK’s Labour debate as timely examples.
Zucman also explains why past wealth taxes, such as France’s, failed and how a well‑designed tax could avoid those pitfalls while raising revenue from the ultra‑rich.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: When You Control the Mail, You Control the Nation
bullets: Rich Baris warns that without building on Trump’s 2024 gains, the GOP coalition will collapse, citing Trump’s foreign‑policy missteps like the Iran war as a key voter grievance.

Trump’s midterm strategy now relies on a national ad blitz—e.g., the “Toughest Guy” spot featuring Dana White—and on funneling his $850 million war chest into select races, while refusing to fund Senate nominee Ken Paxton despite GOP leaders’ pleas.

Senator Blumenthal has asked the USPS to explain a new, untested ballot‑verification system that could reject entire batches of mail‑in votes, a move Trump supports to undermine mail voting ahead of the midterms.

items.subject: Haley Stevens Smears Bernie Sanders and Abdul El-Sayed, Calls Anti-Zionism a ‘Sickness’
bullets: Rep. Haley Stevens, fresh from a Jerusalem visit, called anti‑Zionism a “hate movement” and labeled Bernie Sanders’ Middle‑East stance a “sickness,” while praising Israel despite accusations of genocide in Gaza.

Stevens, who spent over $30 million of AIPAC money on her Michigan Senate race and later endorsed primary loser Abdul El‑Sayed, accused him of “poisonous” anti‑Israel rhetoric even after endorsing him.
Iran claimed retaliation strikes on U.S. allies in Jordan and Iraq after a U.S. airstrike on a wedding killed four civilians, though U.S. Central Command said no troops were killed.

items.subject: Imperialist Delusions and the Price of Fuel
bullets: Trump’s promise to halve fuel prices backfired, with gasoline and diesel soaring as his war with Iran disrupted oil supplies and stretched U.S. military resources.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil facilities for the energy shock, despite those attacks being a response to Russia’s invasion and occurring alongside broader refining bottlenecks.

Krugman notes the Trump administration’s failed attempt to extract Ukrainian mineral revenues, its cut‑off of aid, and its inability to influence Ukraine’s war strategy, highlighting the administration’s weak leverage over fuel prices.

items.subject: Why Won’t Mainstream Media Talk to Hasan Piker?
bullets: Mainstream networks obsess over leftist Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, especially after he campaigned for Democrat Abdul El‑Sayed in Michigan, yet refuse to interview him, turning coverage into “ragebait.”
Piker criticizes the media’s focus on him as a distraction from “unprecedented crises,” arguing it disserves the public and reflects frustration with news outlets.
The newsletter notes a detailed analysis of how many minutes Fox and other networks devote to talking about Piker, highlighting the paradox of extensive coverage without direct engagement.

items.subject: Trump Hands Dems Their Best Gift Yet
bullets: Trump posted on Truth Social that communities shouldn’t want data centers, a move Democrats say weaponizes a growing backlash over rising utility costs and big‑tech influence, turning data centers into a new national ‘third rail’ for the GOP.

Democratic candidates from Wisconsin to Ohio are running TV ads and planning tracker attacks to tie Republican incumbents and Trump to data‑center projects, framing them as anti‑affordability and corruption, while some GOP officials now publicly call for a pause on approvals.

Republican leaders, from Rep. Tom Barrett to Gov. Greg Abbott, are scrambling to distance themselves from Trump’s comment, but the party faces an electoral vulnerability as the data‑center issue fractures coalitions, even prompting unions to warn they won’t back anti‑data‑center candidates.

items.subject: Did Germany’s Green Party Just Try and Get a Screening of Zeteo’s Gaza Doctors Film Canceled?
bullets: The Berlin Greens’ mayoral candidate spokesperson said they would try to influence the cancellation of a Zeteo‑distributed film, ‘Gaza: Doctors Under Attack,’ after the Green‑affiliated Heinrich Böll Institute requested its removal.
Pro‑Israel journalist Wolfgang Tietze wrote to the Greens to urge the cancellation of the film’s screening, which had been acquired by Zeteo following the BBC’s 2023 cancellation of its publication.

items.subject: I’m Launching Something New.
bullets: Sarah Longwell, creator of The Focus Group Podcast, will launch a new Focus Group newsletter for Bulwark+ members, offering deeper analysis of swing voters and key 2026 races based on 400+ focus groups with thousands of voters.
The newsletter promises original, paid‑research insights that explain why voters are shifting—especially former Trump supporters—rather than relying on generic polling or pundit speculation.

items.subject: Trump Just Did an IBGYBG
bullets: The Trump administration is reportedly negotiating a 35% stake in a Venezuelan oil company, granting the U.S. Department of Defense a 100‑year lease and cost‑price oil access, a deal brokered by Alejandro Betancourt López, a chavista oligarch with a history of money‑laundering allegations.

The deal is illegal under U.S. law, which prohibits the Defense Department from owning foreign equity, and under Venezuelan law, which bars foreign governments from holding such stakes, making the arrangement effectively impossible.

The newsletter warns that the Trump‑Betancourt connection is a scandalous example of corruption, urging readers to read the full story for details on Betancourt’s background and the alleged illicit transaction.

items.subject: Meet the Populist Democrat Who Could Help Flip The Senate
bullets: Former Senator Sherrod Brown is challenging GOP incumbent Jon Husted in Ohio’s high‑stakes Senate race, criticizing Husted’s support for data‑center expansion and pledging to champion working‑class voters.
In a Zeteo Substack Live, John Harwood and Brown discuss strategies for Democrats to win back working‑class trust and counter Trump’s “wrecking ball” policies.
The full 14‑minute conversation is available to paid subscribers, with a 1‑minute preview for free readers.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: How Ed Markey Survived the Age War
bullets: The 2024 primary season has seen a generational revolt against the Democratic establishment, with seven long‑time incumbents losing seats to younger, often more progressive challengers across the country.

Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey, an 80‑year‑old progressive with 50 years in Congress, defeated 47‑year‑old centrist Congressman Seth Moulton by 30 points, reversing the usual age‑ideology trend seen elsewhere.

Markey’s victory suggests that in some districts, voters prioritize ideological alignment over age, indicating a potential shift in the Democratic Party’s future direction toward more progressive leadership.

items.newsletter: Here Be Dragons from Barbara F. Walter
items.subject: Why Strongmen Eventually Surround Themselves With Idiots
bullets: Trump’s appointment of inexperienced loyalists—Kristi Noem to DHS, Tulsi Gabbard to the intelligence community, Kash Patel to the FBI, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to HHS, Pete Hegseth to Defense—has caused chaos, a measles outbreak, and weakened key agencies.

Strongmen face a loyalty‑competence trade‑off: once in power, they replace competent officials with loyal, often mediocre, yes‑men, leading to bad policies, economic manipulation, corruption, institutional decay, and higher risk of costly foreign‑policy mistakes.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Mike Johnson, Wet Noodle
bullets: Trump publicly announced a $50.5 million disaster aid package for Texas, praising Governor Abbott and endorsing the state’s Republican ticket, highlighting his overt favoritism toward red states.

Bill Kristol argues the 119th Congress is a “rubber‑stamp” body that blindly supports Trump’s policies, contrasting it with the 1948 “Do‑Nothing” 80th Congress and urging voters to choose Democrats to check those policies.

House Speaker Mike Johnson deflected questions on the Iran war and Pentagon issues, claiming Congress has no role in war decisions, underscoring the GOP’s refusal to exercise its constitutional war‑making responsibilities.

items.subject: Does the shingles vaccine prevent dementia?
bullets: A natural‑experiment study in Wales found shingles vaccination cut dementia risk by about 20% over three years, a result later replicated in Australia, Canada, and US data, though one English hospital‑record study found no link.

The protective effect appears biologically plausible because varicella‑zoster can reactivate silently and cause neuroinflammation, but findings differ by sex and across studies, highlighting the need for randomized trials.
Regardless of dementia benefits, the shingles vaccine is strongly recommended for adults over 50 to prevent the painful, debilitating disease itself.

items.subject: Meet the Gulf ‘Spy Sheikh’ Backing Trump’s Insanely Corrupt Crypto Bank
bullets: Trump’s family crypto firm World Liberty Financial sold a $500 million stake to UAE national security adviser Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed, giving the Emirati a 49% share in the venture and in a pending Trump‑backed bank.

The Trump administration earned at least $1.4 billion from the president’s $TRUMP memecoin and related crypto activities, while simultaneously approving 500,000 AI chips for the UAE and facilitating the Emirati investment.
A UMass Amherst poll found 77% of Americans oppose a sitting president profiting from crypto ventures tied to policy influence, and two‑thirds distrust Trump to avoid such conflicts.

items.subject: The Hits Keep Coming
bullets: Krugman notes U.S. GDP growth and unemployment remain solid despite Trump‑era shocks, but warns that persistent trade wars, Iran conflicts, and rising interest rates threaten future resilience.
He argues that investors’ belief the shocks are one‑time events has kept the economy afloat, yet the auto industry faces existential risk from Canada trade tensions and soaring refined‑fuel prices.
Krugman highlights the U.S. military’s munitions shortages and leadership losses under Hegseth, suggesting future conflicts could further strain economic stability and push rates higher.

items.subject: El-Sayed Asks Michigan’s Jewish Dems for Forgiveness
bullets: Abdul El‑Sayed, Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee, met with Jewish Democratic leaders in Birmingham, apologizing for past remarks that many view as questioning Israel’s right to exist and for his ties to controversial streamer Hasan Piker.

He defended a video statement that condemned a recent synagogue attack but added that U.S. support for Israel’s actions creates a ‘hurt people hurt people’ cycle, sparking further backlash from Jewish voters.

items.newsletter: Tim, Sarah and JVL - The Bulwark
items.subject: Ken Paxton Is Running One of the Worst Campaigns in America
bullets: The Supreme Court temporarily allows Trump’s ballroom to proceed, sparking debate over its future demolition by 2029, while JVL likens Justice John Roberts to Senator Susan Collins for his cautious stance.
Ken Paxton’s campaign is described as one of America’s worst, with Paxton and other Republican incumbents feeling bleak about midterm prospects amid rising voter discontent.
Trump demands punishment for Kristen Welker after she noted his endorsed candidates are losing more often, highlighting intra‑party tensions and the growing scrutiny of Republican messaging.

items.subject: Israeli Raid Forces Gaza Kindergarten to Frantically Evacuate 200 Children
bullets: Israeli forces raided a Gaza City kindergarten, forcing the Red Cross to evacuate 200 children aged 4‑5 amid gunfire and airstrikes near the American Hospital.
Head of the school, Doaa Qadeeh, livestreamed the chaos, pleading for safety as explosions echoed and parents scrambled to rescue their children.
The incident highlights how even supposedly safer Gaza areas are now subject to sudden military operations, endangering young civilians.

items.subject: Sorry, Mr. President. I Have a Thing.
bullets: House Republicans are largely skipping the 2026 RNC in Dallas, citing debates, district duties, and personal reasons, as Trump’s low approval scares vulnerable incumbents in tight races.

The House passed a CR to fund the government through Dec. 11 after infighting over a hemp‑THC amendment and abortion‑funding concerns, delaying the hemp ban to avoid a shutdown during the election year.
Sen. Ted Budd clarified that a brief pro‑forma Senate session is routine to keep the chamber in session, rejecting claims it was a tactic to block Trump’s nominees or commit treason.

items.subject: Lake America and the Dogma of Trumpism
bullets: The author argues that Republican anti‑Canada sentiment, rooted in Trump’s “Lake America” rhetoric, may persist after Trump if the GOP adopts anti‑Canadianism as a political identity, especially if Democrats champion normalization as a repudiation of Trumpism.

If Democrats stay silent on Canada, Republicans might quietly drop the antagonism, but overt Democratic pushes could force GOP politicians to double‑down on anti‑Canadian positions to appeal to their base.

The piece suggests future GOP stances on other Trump‑era policies (e.g., National Guard deployment, monuments, foreign relations) will hinge on whether the party can shed the polarizing Trumpist agenda.

items.subject: How Islamophobia Was Built Into U.S. Policy and Law Even Before 9/11
bullets: Rozina Ali argues that U.S. Islamophobia dates back to the 1940s, with systematic FBI surveillance of Muslim Americans and anti‑terror laws used to target political enemies, not just post‑9/11 threats.
She links the rise of anti‑Muslim bigotry to Cold War policies, Israel’s influence under Benjamin Netanyahu, and the Trump administration’s vague counter‑terrorism statutes.
The newsletter promotes a video interview where Ali details these historical roots and advertises her book *Seasons of Fury* and paid subscription access.

items.subject: Top Dem Influencer: TikTok Censored My Anti-ICE Posts
bullets: Carlos Eduardo Espina, a top Democratic influencer with 23 million followers, claims TikTok censored his anti‑ICE videos, issuing three violation notices in late July after the World Cup.
The flagged videos all addressed ICE or immigration, but were not all new posts, suggesting TikTok may have targeted content based on subject rather than freshness.
Espina, who posts roughly ten videos daily and is well‑versed in TikTok’s guidelines, reports being surprised and confused by the warnings, raising questions about platform moderation practices.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: We Found Her: The Most Absurd General-Election Candidate in America
bullets: Republican candidate Te Mayonna Brown, who won Florida’s 24th District GOP nomination unopposed, appears to be the same person indicted in Illinois for 13 felonies of COVID‑relief fraud, with a trial set weeks after the election.
Court documents link her to the same campaign treasurer, company registrations, and social‑media profiles used in the Illinois run, despite her denial and claim the charges were dropped.
She has raised only about $7,000 and run a minimal campaign in a heavily Democratic district, making her a long‑shot in the November general election.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: Trump (Thankfully) Can't Get Out of His Own Way
bullets: Trump’s political woes—war with Iran, high inflation, low approval, and few legislative wins—are worsened by his own reckless actions that repeatedly sabotage Republican prospects.
His recent blunders, like the absurd attempt to rename Lake Ontario, exemplify how his constant missteps undermine any limited control he has over the political environment.

items.subject: 🤔 Netanyahu Brags How U.S. Cable News Let Him ‘Influence’ America Into War With Iran
bullets: Netanyahu boasted on Israeli TV that his 1,000 hours on US cable news helped persuade America to join a war against Iran, claiming he finally “brought the United States to its senses.”

He reminded listeners that the US has poured over $20 billion into Israel in the past three years despite Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza and attacks on Palestinians and Americans, while American public support for Israel has sharply declined across parties.
The newsletter notes rising tensions with Iran, citing recent US strikes near the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian retaliatory attacks on US bases in Jordan, and Trump’s threats to “smack” Iran further.

items.subject: The Plot to Steal Venezuela’s Oil
bullets: Trump’s secret deal to let U.S. oil firms extract up to 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil hinges on massive infrastructure investment and yields at most $1.3 trillion—tiny versus the U.S.’s $167 trillion wealth—so it adds essentially nothing to the economy or gas prices.

The arrangement, born from a covert kidnapping of Maduro, is a classic 19th‑century resource grab that reinforces U.S. imperialist reputation and faces near‑universal opposition in Venezuela, making its long‑term viability doubtful.

items.subject: Measles deaths debacle, Covid-19 protection for immunocompromised, and more
bullets: The FDA licensed a new Covid‑19 vaccine last week, triggering distribution to clinics and pharmacies with availability expected within two weeks, just as a summer wave spreads exponentially across the West and South.

CDC’s measles death data was inconsistently updated this weekend, shifting from zero to two deaths and then to an asterisk, raising unprecedented questions about data transparency and trust in federal reporting.

Pemgarda, a monoclonal antibody therapy, shows 94% efficacy at three months for immunocompromised patients and offers a long‑acting IV alternative to vaccines, though it requires two infusions 90 days apart and isn’t available in pharmacies.

items.subject: With American Characteristics
bullets: The newsletter claims Trump announced a deal giving the U.S. control of over 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil, allegedly doubling U.S. reserves and lowering gas prices at no taxpayer cost, but the claim is unverified and likely satirical.

Reactions split along partisan lines: Venezuelan opposition calls it colonial extraction, Iran mocks Trump, supporters hail it as strategic genius, while Senator Chris Van Hollen condemns it as endangering service members for billionaire interests.

The author suggests the deal masks a broader U.S strategy using State Department and Pentagon financial networks to counter Chinese influence, arguing the real intent is geopolitical power rather than the advertised oil benefits.

items.subject: U.S. Politicians Reject Donations From Hindu Nationalists, Days After Far-Right RSS Rally in New York
bullets: Nearly 100 U.S. politicians, including Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El‑Sayed, Rep. Ro Khanna and Rep. Pramila Jayapal, have pledged to refuse donations from the RSS after its controversial Madison Square Garden rally.

RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat delivered a “Universal Oneness Celebration” speech in New York, claiming any Hindu who wants no Muslims in Bharat isn’t Hindu, despite his past remarks labeling all Indians as Hindu and blaming Western influence for Indian gang rape.
The rally, organized by a far‑right, Nazi‑inspired Hindu nationalist paramilitary group, sparked large protests outside Madison Square Garden following recent criticism of its extremist ideology.

items.subject: Why MAGA Is Celebrating Milo’s Deportation
bullets: Milo Yiannopoulos was detained by ICE on an expired visa, deported to the UK, and his mugshot was posted by DHS, ending his decade as a right‑wing provocateur; MAGA allies celebrated his removal while liberals mocked his past calls for ICE checkpoints and executions.

Yiannopoulos’s fall was precipitated by a long‑standing feud with Laura Loomer, who reported him to Homeland Security; their split over alliances with Marjorie Taylor Greene and mutual accusations of sexual misconduct fueled the ICE action.

Post‑deportation speculation about Yiannopoulos’s “vault” of damaging material remains unsubstantiated, as he has denied it was a real archive and has not released any evidence, leaving his influence in the alt‑right diminished for now.

items.subject: We could come up short
bullets: Roy Cooper urges donors to give $7 to help his North Carolina Senate campaign reach a $2 million goal and counter GOP attack ads totaling nearly $100 million.
He warns that falling short would jeopardize flipping the seat and allow GOP candidate Michael Whatley, a former Big Oil lobbyist, to win with Trump’s backing.

items.subject: Trump Took the Bait and Walked Straight Into the Data Center Backlash (with Bill Kristol)
bullets: Top military leaders warned the Hegseth think‑tank that prolonged U.S. operations in Iran are unsustainable, citing strain on resources and regional stability.
Will Sommer exposed a Pentagon‑funded “troll army” of propagandists secretly collecting taxpayer money to spin a positive narrative about the Iran situation.

Bill Kristol joins Tim Miller to argue that Trump’s praise of data centers and gifts to Democrats serve tech oligarchs, while Democrats should not let Republicans pass a spending bill that merely keeps the government open.

items.subject: ‘We Aren’t Winning’: Don’t Believe Team Trump’s Iran War Propaganda
bullets: A senior U.S. official told Zeteo the administration’s claim that the Iran war is going well is false, saying ‘we aren’t winning’.
Four officials and a Trump adviser say the Pentagon and broader government believe the war is being lost, and the White House’s propaganda is aimed at boosting Trump’s party before the midterms.
The officials said they are speaking out because they are appalled by what they call ‘nothing but lies and distortions’ in the administration’s public narrative.

items.subject: You Won’t Believe What Marjorie Taylor Greene Did | The Trio
bullets: Milo Yiannopoulos was detained by ICE, with Laura Loomer claiming credit, sparking a chaotic reaction within the MAGA community; the trio highlights the bizarre fallout and internal disputes.
A KKK/Nazi-linked staffer was uncovered in the orbit of Georgia Senate candidate Mike Collins, raising concerns about extremist influence in state politics.
Marjorie Taylor Greene delivered a shocking message to JVL, and Colorado gubernatorial nominee Victor Marx is entangled in a new, perplexing saga, both detailed in the commentary.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: The Cruelty Comes to Springfield
bullets: The U.S. bombed Iranian troops on Larak Island attempting to mine the Strait of Hormuz, killing several, prompting Iranian fire at U.S. bases in Jordan and UAE and nudging oil prices up, while senior military leaders warn Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that large‑scale attacks on Iran are becoming unsustainable.

In Springfield, Ohio, ICE arrested 34 Haitians—including two pastors—over a month, shackling them with ankle monitors despite pending asylum claims, spurring a grassroots mobilization at Greater Grace Temple that organized food, legal aid, and a “Unshackle Springfield” protest.

Activists raised funds for the Haitian Support Center, called Republican officials, and highlighted the historical trauma of ankle monitors, while local clergy and the NAACP condemned the raids as anti‑Black containment and urged community support.

items.subject: Laura Loomer Gets a Pass For Her Racism as the Media Continues to Bash Hasan Piker Instead
bullets: Laura Loomer, a Trump‑aligned activist, called five prominent Black Democratic women—including Ilhan Omar and Ketanji Brown Jackson—‘ghetto Black bitches,’ sparking outrage from Marjorie Taylor Greene but virtually no mainstream media coverage, which the author criticizes for focusing on streamer Hasan Piker instead.

The piece notes Loomer’s deep ties to Trump, citing her role in the 2023 firing of six National Security Council members and her access to the West Wing, while highlighting her recent attacks on a transgender CIA officer and credit for Milo Yiannopoulos’s deportation.

Meanwhile, the author contrasts Loomer’s overt racism with the comparatively muted scrutiny of leftist streamer Hasan Piker’s controversial statements, arguing the media’s double standard reflects a broader bias toward attacking progressive figures.

items.subject: From Kakistocracy to Cheatistocracy
bullets: Krugman argues that U.S. tax policy since the 1950s has eliminated progressive taxes, enabling massive wealth concentration and turning America into a “cheatistocracy” where tax evasion fuels the deficit by over $600 billion annually, about 40% of the federal shortfall.

He cites IRS data showing high‑income audit rates fell from 7.2% in 2011 to 0.7% by 2019 due to a 30‑40% cut in enforcement staff, allowing the ultra‑wealthy to evade taxes at a scale comparable to the entire Medicaid budget.

Krugman notes that while Biden attempted to boost IRS enforcement, Trump’s tax‑cut legislation reversed those gains, further entrenching a system that benefits dishonest billionaires and undermines honest wealth holders.

items.subject: When McCarthyism Hit My Family
bullets: The author links Trump’s recent anti‑immigrant actions—including the January killings of anti‑ICE protesters Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota—to the historic terror of Senator Joseph McCarthy’s anti‑communist crusade.

New York Times‑documented investigations show the Justice Department is probing whether protest‑support groups financed ‘domestic terrorist’ agitators, while instead charging 15 alleged antifa members in Minneapolis, illustrating Trump’s use of federal prosecutors to intimidate Republicans.
The piece reveals the author’s personal family connection to McCarthy‑era repression, drawing a parallel between past anti‑communist witch‑hunts and today’s political violence under Trump.

items.subject: Humbly asking for your support in the toughest reelection campaign in the entire country
bullets: Sen. Jon Ossoff frames his 2026 Georgia Senate race as the GOP’s top target, warning that national Republicans and Super PACs will spend hundreds of millions against him.
He emphasizes that his campaign rejects corporate PAC and lobbyist money, relying on small donor contributions of $10‑$50 to fund voter mobilization, ads, and staff.
Ossoff urges immediate donations via ActBlue, arguing each dollar will directly strengthen the campaign in the highly competitive battleground state.

items.subject: The 2028 Democratic Primary Is Quietly Raging
bullets: Advisors to potential 2028 Democratic candidates are already scouting headquarters locations, with logistical challenges noted for those from Pacific states or places like Louisville, Kentucky.
Strategist Jesse Lehrich warns a fierce scramble for campaign staff, predicting over thirty candidates will compete for top operatives as an early viability signal.

items.subject: Inside Trump’s National Security Dumpster Fire (w/ Julie Curlee)
bullets: Former CIA officer Julie Curlee says Trump’s administration politicized intelligence, removing experienced analysts and eroding nonpartisan expertise, especially on Iran and Venezuela.
Curlee warns that the loss of seasoned public servants could take a generation to repair, as the national security apparatus becomes a “dumpster fire” of politicization.

items.subject: What’s on my mind
bullets: Republican super PACs have poured nearly $100 million into the North Carolina Senate race, targeting Roy Cooper with personal attacks and baseless ads as the seat could shift U.S. Senate control.
Cooper argues that if elected he will hold the Trump administration accountable, prioritize working families, and oppose GOP policies, positioning himself as a key threat to Republican dominance.
He urges supporters to donate before the end‑of‑month deadline to reach a $2 million fundraising goal needed to flip North Carolina blue and regain the Senate for Democrats.

items.subject: Mehdi Challenges Hunter Biden on Gaza, the 2024 Election, Democrats, and His Own Regrets
bullets: Hunter Biden claims his father helped enable Israel’s Gaza genocide, citing a friendship with Netanyahu and admitting his own role in fueling the “Biden crime family” narrative and right‑wing attacks on the family.

He admits battling addiction, discusses his involvement with Hallie Biden and his appearances on Candace Owens and Tucker Carlson, and says he pushed Joe Biden to run for reelection in 2024 while criticizing the Democratic Party’s loyalty and calling Hakeem Jeffries’ secret meeting with Jared Kushner “insanity.”
He hints at a 2028 Democratic nominee pick and says he feels “always disappointed” in the party, while noting his own cancer diagnosis and the ongoing Biden family controversies.

items.subject: Dolly Parton knew there was room for fun in brilliance
bullets: Dolly Parton used self‑aware humor—jokes about her red lips, blonde hair, and “great ass”—to deflect sexist criticism and keep focus on her songwriting, which earned her bestseller status and enduring streams after her death.

Her unapologetic embrace of camp glamour, including playing guitar with long acrylic nails, broke the male‑dominated country music boys’ club and empowered women to write and perform, blending artistry and presentation into a single, influential package.

items.subject: Mike Rogers Wants $50 Copays for Routine Screenings
bullets: Mike Rogers, Michigan Senate candidate, proposes $50 copays for routine screenings and other preventive care, violating current ACA rules that require zero-cost preventive services.

Rogers’ stance reflects a broader GOP push to roll back ACA subsidies and free preventive care, a move that has already driven up premiums for hundreds of thousands of Michiganders and is likely to increase uninsured rates nationwide.

items.subject: Oligarchy and the Great Evasion
bullets: Krugman argues that the U.S. has deliberately dismantled progressive taxation since the 1970s, cutting top individual rates from 90% to 37% and corporate rates from 52% to 21%, while the IRS has been stripped of enforcement resources by Republican congresses.

He estimates the tax gap at $600 billion+ annually—about 40% of the federal deficit—largely driven by high‑income evasion, and claims this unchecked evasion fuels the rise of an oligarchy of the wealthiest 0.01% who now control 19% of all federal political donations.

items.subject: Karoline Leavitt Is Getting Out. Why Would Anyone Want Her Job? (w/ George Conway)
bullets: George Conway critiques Karoline Leavitt’s tenure, accusing her of habitual lying, deflecting, and insulting reporters while defending Trump’s indefensible actions without losing composure.
They discuss potential successors, highlighting CNN’s Scott Jennings as a candidate and questioning whether he could serve as Trump’s next professional gaslighter.

items.subject: This Week in Palestine: Israel Kills 4 Children as It Warns Palestinian Kids Not to Fly Kites
bullets: Israel’s airstrikes on Aug. 22 killed four Gaza children—4‑year‑olds Hassan al‑Hafi and Muhammad Abdel Salam Taha, 10‑year‑old Amal Nash’at Abu Khater, and 14‑year‑old Islam Ahmed Ajouri—while also targeting the West Bank.
Israeli settlers intensified their siege of Qusra, continuing attacks on Palestinian villages and escalating violence in the West Bank, including a severe assault on a 15‑year‑old Palestinian.

The Israeli military’s use of quadcopters and missiles, coupled with ongoing displacement, imprisonment, and starvation, has stripped Gaza’s children of basic childhood activities like kite‑flying, underscoring the regime’s systematic cruelty.

items.subject: Every step of the way
bullets: Governor Roy Cooper urges early voting in 47 days, recalling his eight-year tenure and bipartisan Medicaid expansion that added coverage for hundreds of thousands of North Carolinians.
He highlights personal campaign memories—yard sign sleds, family at inaugural events, and community chats at the State Fair—to emphasize his commitment to working families and trusted leadership.

items.subject: House GOPer in Private Meeting: Trump’s Exhausting Our Voters
bullets: Rep. Stephanie Bice (R‑OK) warned that Trump’s unpopularity and executive actions are eroding GOP support, threatening safe seats and risking voter turnout or split-ticket voting in the midterms.
Bice’s remarks, recorded at an Oklahoma State University event, reveal growing GOP anxiety that Trump’s brand may drive voters to Democrats or cause them to abstain.
The conversation highlights a broader concern among Republican lawmakers that Trump’s leadership is damaging the party’s electoral prospects in traditionally red states.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: How Republicans Came to Dominate the Internet
bullets: In 2008 Obama’s campaign pioneered digital strategy, using data and social media to win; by 2012 Democrats outperformed Republicans with new tech and analytics.
By 2016 the advantage vanished as Trump’s team leveraged Facebook and a growing army of digital media warriors to defeat Clinton, shifting the digital playing field.
Since then Democrats have not regained the lead, falling behind Republicans in effectively navigating and dominating the internet environment.

items.subject: Elected Democrats Are Busy Condemning Hasan Piker While Giving Right-Wing Extremists and Islamophobes a Pass. We H…
bullets: Democratic lawmakers are aggressively condemning leftist Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, falsely labeling him an antisemite for warning against monolithic Zionist narratives, while largely ignoring right‑wing hate figures like Laura Loomer, Jan. 6 rioter Jake Lang, and anti‑Muslim pastor Lorenzo Sewell.

Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider warned that Democrats risk losing credibility by targeting left‑wing figures but failing to denounce right‑wing bigotry, citing the lack of condemnation for Muslim‑targeting rhetoric from candidates such as Abdul El‑Sayed and Mike Rogers.

items.subject: “Nice people are wonderful, but you can’t build a life on being liked”
bullets: Taylor Tomlinson reflects that the youthful “spark” of hypomanic confidence was unsustainable, and now in her thirties she values comfort, safety and genuine connection over fame or constant ambition.

Steve Way argues that true accessibility under the ADA depends on concrete design decisions—not on the fluctuating goodwill of staff—so relying on being liked is an unreliable foundation for basic rights.
Will Cooper describes filleting a wild sea trout in rural England, emphasizing meticulous technique to remove scales and fat for a crisp, dry grill finish.

items.subject: MAGA Is Already Fighting Over 2028. Trump Is Fighting Everyone Else.
bullets: MAGA factions are already battling over the 2028 presidential race, signaling an internal civil war within the movement.
Trump’s confrontation with Iran has undermined his ‘America First’ narrative, exposing contradictions in his foreign policy.
A former Trump aide argues the Natalie Harp controversy was predictable, while warning that Trump may attempt to rig the upcoming midterm elections.

items.subject: Talking Interest Rates with Ricardo Caballero
bullets: Ricardo Caballero argues that the sharp drop in U.S. Treasury yields since 2000 reflects a shortage of safe assets, not a collapse in returns to capital, which have remained relatively stable while the equity risk premium widened.

Caballero contends that the 2008 crisis stemmed from financial engineering that created synthetic safe assets to meet real demand for safety, leading to a post‑crisis surge in Treasury demand and ultra‑low rates.

He disputes the secular stagnation narrative that low rates signal a lack of investment opportunities, pointing out that corporate profit rates and returns on capital did not fall as sharply as safe‑asset yields, undermining the claim of a fundamental productivity slowdown.

items.subject: Why Ed Markey May Survive a Revolt Against Old Candidates (with Adam Reilly)
bullets: Massachusetts voters say Ed Markey’s record and seniority outweigh Rep. Seth Moulton’s “new generation” critique, keeping Markey viable despite a Democratic age revolt.

Moulton’s attacks—including controversial remarks about trans athletes and a contentious AI debate exchange—failed to resonate with focus‑group participants, revealing Democratic voters prioritize policy over generational messaging.

items.subject: This Week in Democracy – Week 84: Trump Admin Plans Largest Visa Revocations in History as ICE Arrests Reach Recor…
bullets: The Trump administration plans to revoke up to 200,000 business and tourist visas for asylum seekers from 2016‑2026, the largest mass visa revocation in U.S. history.
ICE arrested nearly 50,000 people in July—a 15% rise from June and the highest monthly total since Trump returned to office, with 20,000 arrests in Texas and Florida.

The Supreme Court temporarily allowed Trump’s executive order restricting mail‑in voting, but a lower court quickly blocked it again, leaving the case poised for another Supreme Court review as the 2024 midterms approach.

items.subject: Mark Cuban Thinks He Could Run as a Republican. Tim Has Some Bad News.
bullets: Mark Cuban claims he could run for president as a Republican, but Tim argues the GOP lacks the infrastructure and base to support a billionaire outsider, citing his past political missteps and low name recognition.

Sarah discusses her book with the New York Times, revealing her focus on how Democratic voters are shifting toward pragmatic, anti-establishment policies, and she highlights specific policy areas that resonate with them.
Rob Sand’s gubernatorial race in Iowa is examined, noting his moderate stance and the strategic importance of the state’s swing voters for the 2024 election cycle.

items.subject: 6 Months of Trump Iran War Lies, In 7 Charts
bullets: Trump claimed the Iran war would last four weeks, but data shows it has exceeded that timeframe, continuing beyond the projected end date.
Trump dismissed rising gas prices as ‘not very high’, yet EIA data shows a 30% increase from $3 to over $4 per gallon, peaking at $4.60 in May 2026.
The newsletter critiques Trump’s narrative that the war is a U.S. triumph, presenting statistics that contradict his assertions of safety, wealth, and progress.

items.subject: Dolly Parton’s Literacy Miracle
bullets: Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library has delivered over 332 million books to nearly 3.2 million children, but recent state budget cuts in Indiana, Kentucky, Maine, and Missouri threaten its funding.

The program relies heavily on government grants; Indiana eliminated its match, Kentucky proposed halving support before restoring it after backlash, Maine lost funding entirely, and Missouri cut $4 million for 2027.
The author urges politicians to champion increased public funding for the Imagination Library and invites readers to donate via local partner organizations.

items.subject: How Dems Can Win on Immigration in November
bullets: A Reuters/Ipsos poll shows only 37% approve of Trump’s immigration handling, opening a 19‑point gap Democrats could exploit by framing immigration as pro‑worker and economically beneficial","Winning Jobs Narrative research found two top messages boost Democratic support by ~2 points: highlighting immigrant tax contributions versus billionaire gains, and contrasting ICE spending with cuts to food/health benefits","The memo warns Democrats to avoid four traps—silence, pure compassion without economics, harm‑only narratives, and over‑emphasizing enforcement—and instead use faith‑leader‑style, economic‑interdependence messaging to win working‑class voters.

items.subject: ‘I Am an American Citizen Under Siege by Israeli Settler Extremists’
bullets: American Ohio resident Loui Ridi was trapped in his Qusra home for nearly three weeks as Israeli settlers encircled the house, while U.S.‑funded Israeli soldiers and the Israeli military declared the area a closed zone, preventing residents from leaving or meeting neighbors.

Ridi planted an American flag on his rooftop to deter settlers, who would raise a yellow flag if they took over; U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee condemned the siege but no substantive action was taken to stop the settlers.

items.subject: Pounding the pavement and putting on the mileage
bullets: Roy Cooper’s Senate campaign is touring North Carolina to highlight rising costs of groceries, gas, and housing, urging voters that “stuff costs too much” and Washington is indifferent.
He asks supporters to donate $5 to meet a $2 million fundraising deadline by Monday night, needed to fund travel, gas, materials, and organizers for the final 70‑day push.
Cooper cites his record as governor—expanding Medicaid, raising teacher pay, creating jobs, and adding paid parental leave—as proof he will put people before power in the Senate.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: A Dream Delayed Will Not Be a Dream Denied
bullets: Bill Kristol recounts a moving scene at Reagan National Airport where WWII, Korean, and Vietnam veterans were honored by spontaneous standing ovations, symbolizing a hopeful unity between veterans of democracy and civil rights.

He contrasts this moment of national solidarity with the current administration’s perceived regression of civil rights, arguing that the president’s policies threaten the promises of the Constitution and the American dream.

Kristol urges readers to remember Martin Luther King Jr.’s 1963 speech and to believe that, despite recent setbacks, the nation can once again achieve the freedom and equality promised by the founding documents.

items.subject: Two more kids die. And one more theater show.
bullets: The 2023 measles outbreak in West Texas, fueled by underfunded local health departments, grew to over 900 reported cases—likely ten times higher—causing two child deaths and sparking a national anti‑vaccine backlash featuring RFK Jr.’s Children’s Health Defense and misleading media narratives about the cause of death.

In Pennsylvania, two more children died from measles this week amid a chaotic response that included political interference, poor communication, and targeted attacks on vaccine trust, illustrating how systemic failures continue to endanger lives.

items.subject: 💻🤪 How Stephen Miller Uses Natalie Harp to Help Trump Ratchet Up the Crazy
bullets: Natalie Harp, a 35‑year‑old aide, now controls Trump’s Truth Social feed, feeding him agitprop and acting as the de‑facto replacement for longtime social‑media chief Dan Scavino.

Senator Jon Ossoff highlighted Harp’s unusual influence, prompting a White House backlash and underscoring how senior officials now route social‑media requests through her instead of texting the president directly.

Six months after Trump’s promised four‑week war with Iran, he appears disengaged, while Harp’s role in amplifying MAGA messaging grows amid ongoing ethnic‑cleansing reports in places like Springfield, Ohio.

items.subject: Make Geography Great Again
bullets: Krugman mocks Trump's alleged plans to rename geographic features, proposing absurd alternatives like 'Lethality Ocean' for the Pacific and 'European Heritage Sea' for the Black Sea.
He frames the piece as a tongue‑in‑cheek 'day off' written after a rainy, exhausting drive, highlighting the satire rather than serious policy analysis.

items.subject: MAGA’s 2028 Civil War Is Already Here
bullets: JD Vance’s team believes a coordinated “op” on X and behind‑the‑scenes is trying to sabotage his bid for the 2028 GOP nomination, sparking paranoia among his allies.

Vance insiders, citing a Trump‑aligned source, say the anti‑Vance effort signals escalating Republican infighting in the post‑Trump era, with the plot framed as a deliberate digital manipulation campaign.

items.subject: Maîtres Chez Nous
bullets: Prime Minister Mark Carney invoked Quebec’s 1962 “Maîtres Chez Nous” slogan during a press conference to frame the US‑Canada trade collapse as an existential, nationalist fight, echoing historic anti‑anglophone sentiment.
Carney’s move signals a hard‑line stance to protect politically sensitive domestic industries amid Trump‑driven trade tensions, betting on upcoming US midterms to pressure a favorable deal.
The author warns that Carney’s recent shift from climate advocate to hydrocarbon ally foreshadows a pipeline construction boom in Canada, reshaping global energy flows.

items.subject: The Dawn of FAFO Economics
bullets: A CBS News/YouGov poll finds nearly two‑thirds of Americans, including 54% of Republicans, support government price controls on goods and services.
The author warns that historical examples—from the Soviet Union to 1970s U.S.—show price controls cause shortages and black markets, contradicting claims by Trump and Elizabeth Warren.
Despite lacking evidence, politicians are pushing price‑setting policies, banking on public opinion rather than economic analysis.

items.subject: How Trump Lost the Iran War in Every Way Possible in Less Than 6 Months
bullets: Trump’s “40‑day war” against Iran failed to stop Tehran’s attacks on regional shipping, and after four months of half‑hearted bombings and two U.S. blockades, Iran now controls roughly a third of Strait of Hormuz traffic and shoots at “unauthorized” vessels with impunity.

The administration shifted from impossible regime‑change goals to a more realistic, yet horrifying, aim of regime collapse, a strategy embraced by Netanyahu but abandoned by Trump after Kurdish uprisings faltered, culminating in an April ceasefire that tacitly admitted bombing could not destroy the Iranian state.

Former DNI Tulsi Gabbard warned regime change was unrealistic and that Iran would close the Strait, while Joint Chiefs Chairman Dan Caine cautioned limited air‑defense munitions and U.S. casualty risks, yet Trump persisted in a war to reopen the strait and lower gas prices, ultimately losing on all fronts within six months.

items.subject: Sam Stein Used to Be a Thief
bullets: Tim Miller and guest Sam Stein debate the surge in ICE arrests, citing a New York Times article that shows a sharp rise in detentions across the U.S. and questioning Trump’s immigration policy.

They rank Republican officials, calling Marco Rubio a catastrophe, RFK Jr. a failure, and Kelly Loeffler “proof that aliens exist” after a viral video, while noting DeSantis’s alleged Medicaid scandal and Florida’s alleged dirty dealings.

items.subject: We Are Not Prepared for Election-Denying Swing State Governors
bullets: Republican gubernatorial candidates in swing states, including Pennsylvania’s Stacy Garrity, have backed Trump’s 2020 election fraud claims, threatening electoral integrity if they win.
Garrity trails incumbent Gov. Josh Shapiro by 16 points among likely voters in a NYT poll, yet gained Trump’s endorsement through a direct phone call, boosting her profile.
If election‑denying governors win in key swing states, the 2028 presidential election could face heightened risks of contested results and weakened democratic norms.

items.subject: Conflating Jews with Israel Is Dangerous – Whether by Antisemites, U.S. Politicians, or the Israeli State
bullets: U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden ruled that the Star of David on Israel’s flag symbolizes the Jewish race, rejecting the claim that the flag represents only the state and not Judaism.

The author argues that conflating the Israeli flag with Jewish identity fuels antisemitism, noting surveys where 61% of American Jews see Israel committing war crimes and only 36% tie support for Israel to their Jewish identity.
He likens the misuse of religious symbols on national flags to blaming all Jews for Israel’s actions, just as all Muslims are unfairly blamed for extremist groups.

items.subject: 💬 New thread from Citrini Analyst Team
bullets: Nvidia’s new ACIE segment generated $40 billion in Q2 sales, up 138% YoY, confirming the Enterprise Sovereignty thesis that enterprises, sovereigns, and neoclouds are becoming key AI accelerator buyers.

Nutanix is moving inference in-house, eliminating per‑token costs, and now supports its Cloud Platform on third‑party arrays (Dell, NetApp, Lenovo, Everpure), driving new 7‑figure ACV deals as enterprises repatriate workloads.

Everpure reported 38% YoY revenue growth and 77% operating profit increase, raising FY2027 guidance above $5 billion and emphasizing “data primacy” – full sovereignty over enterprise data for AI services.

items.subject: Pete Hegseth Is Building a Pentagon Troll Army
bullets: DataRepublican, the online alias of Utah mom Jennica Pounds, has been a temporary special government employee at the Pentagon since July, a fact revealed after she falsely accused State Dept. official Sarah B. Rogers of treason.

Pounds’s secret Pentagon role raises concerns about her politically charged posts, including attacks on former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, and suggests Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth may be using extremist influencers to target opponents, potentially breaching ethical norms.

items.subject: The Barometer LIVE! On Mondays with Rebekah Jones starting Sept. 14
bullets: The author will host a live three‑hour Monday morning stream starting Sept 14, 7‑10 am, covering news, science, tech and social media with guest experts, broadcast on Substack, YouTube and other platforms, with call‑in participation.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Trump’s Coming Midterm Crashout
bullets: The author predicts a decisive midterm defeat for Trump and Republicans on Nov 4, with the GOP likely losing the House and possibly the Senate, ending Trump’s legislative agenda and sparking intense scrutiny.
Polls show Trump’s key issue approval on border security at -5 and a 49% strong disapproval versus only 17% strong approval, indicating deep voter frustration and a widening enthusiasm gap.

Trump is urging voters to pretend he’s on the ballot while warning that Republican candidates depend on his endorsement, but the author warns this strategy will backfire and lead to a post‑midterm ‘crashout.’

items.subject: It’s a team effort
bullets: Roy Cooper urges weekly $5 donations, saying small recurring gifts let the campaign plan ads, voter outreach, and get‑out‑the‑vote efforts in September‑October as GOP spends nearly $100 million against him
He frames the race as a fight for North Carolina working families, warning that Republican dark‑money allies aim to install Michael Whatley in the U.S. Senate

items.subject: Macro Memo: Regime Change
bullets: Citrini argues that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh are coordinating a regime change that will shrink the Fed’s balance sheet while expanding bank leverage through liquidity regulation reform, enabling banks to count prepositioned discount‑window collateral as liquid assets and thus issue more loans and securities.

The plan hinges on a new Treasury‑Fed Accord 2.0 that increases Treasury bill issuance to reduce long‑duration USTs, lower coupons, and boost private‑sector growth, with the Treasury selling bills instead of bonds and the Fed buying them.

Citrini cites the SVB collapse as evidence that banks lacking proper discount‑window positioning are vulnerable, and argues that recognizing contingent liquidity will transform the banking system by allowing banks to hold less high‑quality liquid assets while maintaining the same LCR, thereby expanding the money supply without tightening monetary policy.

items.subject: Inside Team Trump’s Plan to Use Michael Cohen to Go After Trump’s Enemies
bullets: Team Trump is reportedly planning to weaponize former fixer Michael Cohen, now seeking a federal pardon, as part of a strategy to target political enemies.

The author recounts Cohen’s past threats against a Daily Beast reporter, his federal raid, and his role as a key witness in both Letitia James’s civil fraud case and Alvin Bragg’s criminal hush‑money case against Trump.
The newsletter also notes anti‑vax activist Robert F. Kennedy Jr. deflecting blame for two measles deaths in Pennsylvania and Trump’s upcoming interview with Glenn Beck.

items.subject: Biden Derangement Syndrome
bullets: Krugman argues that the U.S. economy improved under Biden, with inflation falling and growth surpassing other advanced economies, but has deteriorated since Trump’s return, citing slower growth, higher inflation, and rising inequality.

He accuses Trump’s allies of ‘Biden derangement syndrome,’ blaming Biden for current problems like high gas prices and a weak economy, while noting Trump’s unfulfilled promises to cut energy and grocery costs.

Krugman warns that Trump’s economic failures are self-inflicted and that the administration’s attempts to blame Biden are desperate, suggesting the political damage will affect Trump’s November approval ratings.

items.subject: How Can CNN’s Dana Bash Pretend to Be an Objective Journalist Anymore?
bullets: CNN anchor Dana Bash appeared on Bill Maher’s show, nodding to his harsh criticism of Democrats for supporting pro‑Palestinian causes and labeling them as bigoted, while dismissing Gaza as not a genocide.
Bash’s comments echoed a pattern of partisan bias, aligning with Maher’s pro‑Israel stance and questioning Democratic motives, despite the network’s claim of objective journalism.
The episode highlights growing accusations that Bash’s reporting on Israel‑Gaza is heavily slanted, undermining her credibility as an impartial journalist.

items.subject: Trump Is Racing to Build His Ballroom Before the Courts Stop Him (Andrew Weissmann)
bullets: Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts let construction of the White House ballroom proceed, a move the hosts say aids Trump’s fundraising and legacy building before potential legal setbacks.
A recent court ruling limits Trump’s ability to expand mail‑in voting, which the hosts argue could curb his electoral influence in upcoming contests.

They highlight Greg Abbott’s refusal to extradite an ICE officer accused of shooting a man and lying, and note a traveler who wiped his phone to avoid a border search, underscoring tensions over law‑enforcement accountability.

items.subject: Prepare for Trump to Try to Steal the Midterms
bullets: The Supreme Court temporarily stayed a lower‑court injunction, giving Trump a procedural win but not a blanket permission to direct the Postal Service on mail‑in ballot eligibility, while broader election‑security battles loom as early voting starts in as little as four weeks.

Trump’s administration has pressured states for voter‑registration rolls, threatened to suspend ICE operations for sanctuary compliance, and urged Republican gerrymandering, while hinting at using ICE, the National Guard, or the Insurrection Act to influence polling places ahead of the midterms.

Despite being weakened, Trump continues to claim the 2020 election was compromised, targeting officials like CISA chief Christopher Krebs and promoting unfounded foreign‑interference narratives, signaling he may still attempt overt or covert actions to subvert the November vote.

items.subject: EXCLUSIVE: The Right’s ‘War on Woke’ Is a Cash Grab on State Treasuries
bullets: The State Financial Officers Foundation (SFOF) is a nonprofit that brings Republican state treasurers, auditors, right‑wing activists, and Christian finance executives together to steer state treasury money toward faith‑aligned firms and fossil‑fuel interests, while publicly opposing climate‑mitigation efforts.

Derek Kreifels, former CEO of SFOF, now lobbies treasurers to invest public retirees’ savings in his firm Prospr Aligned and its affiliates; his company has already secured contracts with the Kentucky auditor’s office and is targeting Alaska’s Permanent Fund through connections with former Revenue Commissioner Adam Crum and Chair Jason Brune.

SFOF has funded travel for state officials to Prospr’s New York Stock Exchange launch party and arranged for Trump‑SEC chairman Paul Atkins to speak, illustrating the organization’s role in promoting Kreifels’s private business ventures at the expense of public funds.

items.subject: True Confessions of a Sports Dad
bullets: The author argues youth sports should be pursued only for fun or potential money, warning against using them as college résumé boosters, and stresses early talent is obvious, citing a 5th‑grader cross‑country prodigy who later ranked top‑50 nationally.

He claims elite ability appears at a very young age—examples include a 16‑year‑old who could bat like a future first‑round MLB draft pick and a 12‑year‑old club champion who later reached the PGA Tour—so if a child isn’t clearly exceptional, they should prioritize enjoyment.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: Did Trump Just Put South Carolina in Play?
bullets: Trump backed Darline Graham, a political novice appointed by the governor, spending nearly $1 million via his Super PAC, leading to her narrow primary win in South Carolina.
Pfeiffer admits he hoped Graham would lose, expecting it to signal Trump’s waning influence, but her victory may make her a vulnerable incumbent in the general election.
He warns that Trump’s aggressive support for Graham could inadvertently open a path for Democrats to capture the Senate seat for the first time in 28 years.

items.subject: Is Trump’s War Handing Democrats Their Next Win?
bullets: Favreau argues that the unpopular war in Ukraine under Trump mirrors the 2003 Iraq war, creating a political opening for Democrats similar to the 2006 midterms that led to Obama’s election
He cites polling showing a majority of Americans view the war as a mistake and that Democratic candidates who position themselves against it could gain significant swing‑state support
Favreau warns that Democrats must seize the moment quickly, framing the conflict as a moral and fiscal failure of the GOP to turn public discontent into electoral gains

items.subject: Let’s talk about this chaotic trade war and voting rights
bullets: Cooper warns that renewed U.S. tariffs on Canada—North Carolina’s top export market—are squeezing small farms and businesses, raising consumer prices and hurting profit margins.

He claims North Carolina Republicans, backed by a new Supreme Court‑enabled unlimited‑spending tool, are restricting early voting, removing ballot boxes from campuses, and curbing Sunday voting to suppress turnout.
Cooper urges grassroots donations and volunteer efforts to counter the tariffs and voting restrictions ahead of the midterm election.

items.subject: This Cancer Breakthrough Has Scientists Cheering—and Crying
bullets: Catherine Wu’s 2009 hypothesis at Dana‑Farber was that tumor‑specific mutations could be used to train the immune system to recognize and kill cancer cells, potentially enabling personalized vaccines.
The NIH funded Wu’s $363,000 grant in 2009, one of 5,300 that year, betting on this long‑shot idea; fifteen years later, breakthroughs in tumor‑specific immunotherapy suggest the investment paid off.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Trump Is Weaker Than Ever
bullets: Trump’s endorsed candidates barely won South Carolina Senate runoff (52‑48) and Oklahoma governor’s race by half a point, showing his influence is waning even within GOP primaries.
A new Reuters‑Ipsos poll shows only 33% overall approve of Trump’s performance, with 18% of Republicans disapproving and just 35% giving him strong approval, indicating slipping support.
Despite his weakened political standing, Kristol warns Trump remains dangerously megalomaniacal, pursuing authoritarian projects and likely to try subverting the 2024 midterms.

items.newsletter: Here Be Dragons from Barbara F. Walter
items.subject: Why Is Trump Wrecking the Economy Before the Midterms?
bullets: Trump’s recent 50% tariffs on Canadian goods, aggressive immigration restrictions, and support for the Iran‑Israel war have pushed inflation and gas prices up, causing 64% of voters to disapprove of his handling of inflation and giving Democrats an eight‑point lead on cost‑of‑living plans ahead of the midterms.

The Congressional Budget Office estimates Trump’s immigration policies will add $500 billion to deficits over ten years, while the GOP’s 2023 tax‑and‑spending bill is projected to increase the federal deficit by $4.7 trillion over the next decade, contradicting his pledge to slash spending.

Walter argues Trump is accelerating these unpopular policies now because his Republican‑controlled Congress and Senate give him a narrow window to lock in his preferred agenda before Democrats regain power, even if it harms Republican electoral prospects.

items.subject: Dems Obsess Over Hasan Piker, Give Trump and Rogers a Pass
bullets: Democratic leaders are spending weeks attacking left‑wing podcaster Hasan Piker for remarks that Jews aren’t monolithic in supporting Israel, using the controversy to pressure Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El‑Sayed despite his anti‑genocide stance and $32 million AIPAC opposition.

The piece argues Democrats are prioritising pro‑Israel signaling over confronting Trump’s “deeply corrupt, fascist” administration, even as Trump’s trade war with Canada escalates and Republican Darline Graham wins a South Carolina Senate runoff.

It suggests the focus on Piker serves to marginalise anti‑Israel voices and distract from broader electoral threats, implying Democrats care less about defeating Trump than about appeasing Israel’s unpopular policies.

items.subject: Your guide to fall 2026 vaccines
bullets: Fall 2026 respiratory vaccines—flu, RSV, and Covid‑19—will be free; flu vaccine covers three updated strains, offered by five manufacturers, and reduces doctor visits by 30‑60%

RSV vaccines for adults 50+ (GSK, Pfizer, Moderna) and for pregnancy (Pfizer’s ABRYSVO) are available; infants under 8 months should receive monoclonal antibodies (nirsevimab or clesrovimab) unless mother had a pregnancy RSV vaccine
Co‑administration of flu and Covid‑19 vaccines is safe and convenient; all fall vaccines are free and can be given together, with no major safety concerns reported

items.subject: Der Untergang
bullets: Krugman warns that Trump’s ego, disconnection from reality, and unprecedented deference from federal machinery threaten U.S. global standing, eroding trust, weakening military credibility, and inviting ridicule by smaller states.

He likens Trump’s impending loss of power to Hitler’s final days, suggesting Trump may retaliate by damaging national symbols and infrastructure—e.g., the White House’s South Lawn and gilded statues—mirroring Hitler’s Nero Decree.

Krugman argues that even after Trump leaves, the world will remember America’s willingness to elect such a leader, undermining its reputation and leaving the nation vulnerable to future political instability.

items.subject: Dolly Parton Dies at 80. Here Are 9 Ways She Changed America and the World for the Better
bullets: Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, launched in 1995, has distributed over 325 million free books to children under five across the U.S., Canada, U.K., Ireland and Australia, boosting early literacy while facing state‑funding battles in Missouri, Indiana, Kentucky and Maine.

Her Dollywood Foundation’s Buddy Program, begun in the early 1990s, cut Sevier County high‑school dropout rates from 35 % to 6 % by guaranteeing $500 scholarships to 7th‑ and 8th‑graders who graduated, and the foundation continues to fund scholarships and educational initiatives.

items.newsletter: Tim, Sarah and JVL - The Bulwark
items.subject: All MAGA Media Can Talk About Now is Trans Sports
bullets: The hosts mourn Dolly Parton’s death, assess America’s ongoing trade war with Canada and argue the US can’t be relied on internationally even if Democrats win in 2028.
They analyze the South Carolina Senate runoff, questioning whether Donald Trump’s endorsement alone can lift a political novice, and note Pennsylvania’s first measles death of the year.

They critique MAGA media’s obsession with trans issues in the WNBA, debate a rumored Trump administration plan to demolish the Kennedy Center, and discuss JVL’s triad on Trump’s bizarre relationship with Natalie Harp.

items.subject: I Worked for Trump. The Natalie Harp Saga Isn’t Surprising.
bullets: The newsletter claims that Natalie Harp’s close proximity to President Trump and her role in relaying messages from senators reveal a pattern of unusual power dynamics and obsequious behavior, including her sending overly flattering letters to the president.

The author, who has personal experience working in Trump’s environment, argues that Harp’s situation is not unique but part of a broader trend of Trump’s staff being expected to perform extreme, often humiliating tasks—such as steaming his pants while he was still wearing them—to gain favor and access.

items.subject: ‘Nerd Reich’ Author Exposes What Far-Right Tech Bosses Actually Want
bullets: Peter Thiel’s 2010 talk framed technology as a way to bypass elections, suggesting Silicon Valley’s elite view democracy as a barrier to their power and aim for a tech‑run future.

Journalist Gil Durán argues that Silicon Valley’s “Nerd Reich” believes the U.S. will collapse and that tech moguls are actively trying to trigger that collapse, a claim explored in his book and interview.

items.subject: The Atheist Congressman Taking On MAGA’s Nationalist Crusaders
bullets: Rep. Jared Huffman (D‑Calif.) released *No Prophets*, a book exposing how radical Christian nationalist groups like Rad Trads and Theo Bros helped fuel the Jan 6 insurrection and how many GOP officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, are linked to such sects

Huffman, a self‑identified humanist, argues Congress has created a permissive environment for Christian‑based extremist activism and urges figures like Sen. Raphael Warnock to champion church‑state separation despite political risks

Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton, facing weak polling and donor fatigue, pivoted to an anti‑AI data‑center platform—banning Chinese tech, criminal liability for child harm, and rural bans—while receiving sizable contributions from data‑center interests such as Valero, CRH Americas, Sago Energy, and Tyler Winklevoss

items.subject: Why ‘We Need To Tax Billionaires’
bullets: Zucman’s research shows U.S. and European billionaires often pay near‑zero income tax by routing earnings through offshore holding companies, with French billionaires taxed at only 1.25% on €3 billion dividends versus 30% for ordinary shareholders.

New data from tax‑return collaborations reveal that even iconic figures like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos sometimes receive tax credits despite massive wealth, highlighting a systemic loophole where the ultra‑rich effectively make income tax optional.

A wealth tax on ultra‑high‑net‑worth individuals is proposed as the next democratic step, since billionaire tax contributions currently represent a negligible share of national revenue (e.g., 0.03% loss if French billionaires fled offshore).

items.subject: Trump vs. The Leaders of the Free World
bullets: The author argues that the United States has effectively lost its status as the “leader of the free world,” with Trump’s America actively opposing the liberal order it once championed.

Citing a Bulwark Daily podcast where Tim called former Bank of England governor Mark Carney a ‘leader of the free world’ for confronting the U.S. president, the piece suggests that new leadership is emerging outside America.
According to the author, a ‘triumvirate’ of non‑U.S. figures now guides the free world’s future as liberal democracies organize to defend themselves from Trump’s policies.

items.subject: A tough update
bullets: JD Vance visited North Carolina, Trump attacked Cooper on Truth Social, and Stephen Miller criticized him on Fox News, fueling negative coverage.
Republicans have spent nearly $100 million in the race and the GOP super PAC launched false attack ads, while a recent poll shows the contest is statistically tied.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Everyone, Take a Deep Breath About That SCOTUS Decision
bullets: ICE deported Cristy Maryori Villafranca‑Trejo, a Honduran immigrant and wife of an Army sergeant, after a targeted enforcement operation, highlighting the Trump administration’s aggressive deportation policy that has removed over fifty military spouses with no criminal records

items.subject: 🐂 Abdul El-Sayed Went on Fox and Cut Through Jesse Watters's Bullshit
bullets: Abdul El‑Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan, held a 26‑minute Fox interview with Jesse Watters, managing to shut down the host and score points by mocking Republican opponent Mike Rogers as a “beta” and highlighting his 11‑to‑1 spending disadvantage against Rep. Haley Stevens backed by AIPAC.

El‑Sayed deflected Watters’ culture‑war attacks, turning the conversation toward substantive issues like healthcare, inequality and cost‑of‑living, while also dismissing accusations about sharia law by likening it to canon law.

The newsletter notes that while Trump’s trade war with Canada continues and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced new Iran sanctions, the administration remains reluctant to confront China or Russia over their trade with Tehran.

items.subject: Losing the Iran War: The Economic Front
bullets: Trump’s claim that Iran is defeated and a deal imminent is false; the U.S. is trying to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, but estimates of 8 million barrels per day are unreliable and the strategic impact is limited.

U.S. military setbacks in the Gulf have left it unable to protect allies, so Iran can likely expand attacks on regional oil infrastructure, while refined‑product price spikes persist due to global refining shortages, not crude prices.
China can easily offset U.S. sanctions—its economy dwarfs Iran’s ($45 billion export revenue is 0.2% of China’s GDP)—making any U.S. attempt to economically isolate Iran implausible.

items.subject: Foodborne illness increase? Common cold, Covid-19 summer wave, and more.
bullets: Common colds are rising as schools reopen, with peak runny noses expected by mid‑September, while Covid‑19 wastewater levels are low nationally but sharply increasing in the West and South, especially affecting children under five and adults over 65.

Food recall counts this year (483) are average, but recall volume jumped 2,432% to 37.18 million lbs—driven by a massive Cyclospora outbreak—suggesting possible under‑detection of foodborne illness despite stable recall numbers.

A personalized mRNA melanoma therapy showed markedly lower recurrence and death risk in early trials, and the U.S. age‑adjusted death rate fell 4.6% in 2025 versus 2024, though declines lag for American Indians and Alaska Natives.

items.subject: A MAGA Propaganda Circular Firing Squad
bullets: Jennica Pounds, known as “Data Republican,” claimed a State Department undersecretary, Sarah B. Rogers, tried to trap her into leaking Cuba documents, risking treason charges.
The allegation is odd because Pounds is a Trump‑administration favorite who rose to fame for dubious data claims about Elon Musk’s cuts to USAID during the DOGE era.
The piece suggests Rogers, praised by MAGA for defending far‑right speech in Europe, may be embroiled in a bizarre internal conspiracy, prompting a Bulwark+ subscription pitch.
