items.subject: A Tale of Two Genocides: The West’s Hypocrisy in Gaza Desecrates Remembrance in Myanmar
bullets: Rohingya Genocide Remembrance Day marks the 2017 Myanmar “clearance operations” that displaced 1.2 million Rohingya to Bangladesh and killed an estimated 30,000 people.

The U.S. formally declared the attacks genocide on March 21 2022 after interviewing refugees and reviewing soldier whistleblowers, finding orders to shoot indiscriminately, burn villages, rape women and use racial slurs.

The newsletter argues Western condemnation of Myanmar’s atrocities starkly contrasts with its muted response to Israel’s actions in Gaza, highlighting a double standard in applying the Genocide Convention.

items.subject: Canada’s Message to Trump: Kiss My Ass
bullets: Trump’s claim of a U.S.-Canada trade deficit is mathematically flawed, as Canada runs a surplus with the U.S. and the two economies are tightly integrated, especially in autos.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford retorted to Trump’s trade attacks with a profane “kiss my ass” message, while Prime Minister Mark Carney pivots toward deeper EU economic ties to offset U.S. pressure.
Analysts warn the escalating tariff war could backfire on American workers and consumers by disrupting the cross‑border auto supply chain and raising prices.

items.subject: Trump and Natalie: A F*cked-Up Love Story
bullets: The Daily Beast uncovered a 2017 96‑second video by Natalie J. Harp, in which she claims a 2015 sterile‑water infusion caused hemorrhagic shock, cancer and chronic pain, and credits Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign rhetoric with saving her life.

Harp later expanded this narrative in a 2019 LinkedIn essay, further dramatizing her alleged medical tragedy and positioning Trump as a heroic figure for “the forgotten,” suggesting a fabricated, self‑promotional mythos.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: The Jeffries-Kushner Meeting: What It Actually Means
bullets: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries met privately with Trump’s son‑in‑law Jared Kushner in New York, a secretive discussion arranged by a mutual friend, according to five sources.
The meeting, described as a broad conversation on various topics, was timed as Republicans anticipate a Democratic‑led House and seek to build a working relationship before any power shift.
Democrats, including figures like Mehdi Hasan, reacted with intense anger, accusing Jeffries of legitimizing a corrupt figure, while only a few party members defended the engagement.

items.subject: Mehdi Debates Pete Hegseth’s Christian Nationalist Pastor Ally
bullets: Mehdi confronts Pastor Douglas Wilson, a self‑described Christian nationalist linked to Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, over his vision to repeal the 19th Amendment, ban gay marriage and bar non‑Christians from office, arguing the Constitution contains no Christian references.

Wilson defends a book calling slavery a “mutual affection” relationship, claims states keeping gay marriage should be expelled, and asserts the U.S. was founded as a Christian nation, all of which Mehdi fact‑checks with historical evidence.

items.subject: My advice for students heading back to school
bullets: Senator Roy Cooper, son of a longtime public‑school teacher, emphasizes his lifelong support for public education and promises to continue advocating for schools in the U.S. Senate.
He offers back‑to‑school advice: accept nervousness, get involved in activities, eat a good breakfast, be kind, and, if able, help supply drives since teachers often fund classroom needs themselves.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Reality TV Cabinet Secretary Has No Grasp of Reality
bullets: The New York Times reports a Russian autonomous drone killed three civilians in Zaporizhzhia, marking possibly the first fatalities from an AI‑controlled weapon system.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy defended Trump’s renewed tariff war with Canada, falsely claiming Canada lacks a military and attacking its euthanasia policy, despite Canada’s historic wartime contributions and lower suicide rate.
The Wall Street Journal editorial called Trump’s escalation of the Canada tariff dispute “the dumbest trade war,” saying it makes no economic or political sense.

items.subject: 🍁 It’s a Huge Scandal That Trump Is Plunging Us Into ‘War’ With Canada
bullets: Trump’s administration has escalated an economic war with Canada, re‑imposing tariffs and derailing trade talks, prompting Canadian leaders to question the U.S.–led global order.
The newsletter links Trump’s “Economic D‑Day” with Iran and criticizes Hakeem Jeffries for a secret meeting with Jared Kushner, framing both as part of the broader conflict.

items.subject: The Moose That Roared
bullets: Trump imposed steep tariffs on Canadian goods, prompting Canada to ban U.S. alcohol sales and walk out of renegotiations, escalating a trade war despite Canada’s smaller economy.
Krugman argues the U.S. depends heavily on Canadian imports—lumber, heavy crude, hydropower, and auto parts—so a full trade war would hurt America more than Canada.
He predicts Trump will lose the trade war, as Canadians are willing to bear the pain while American public opinion turns against his economic policies.

items.subject: Tim and Will Tour Where MAGA Goes to Party, Fight & Get Arrested
bullets: Tim Miller returns to DC for a chaotic tour of MAGA hotspots, including a $500,000 membership club co‑founded by Donald Trump Jr. and a bar where Rand Paul’s son was seen with Rep. Mike Lawler.
Will Sommer’s scavenger‑hunt guide also visits a strip‑mall club where Bessent allegedly threatened Bill Pulte and even checks out Mitch McConnell’s house, though it’s unclear who’s inside.

items.subject: Trump Needs to Channel His Inner George Constanza to End His Disastrous Iran War
bullets: Six months into the U.S. war with Iran, the author argues President Trump appears clueless, making decisions that consistently backfire and reveal flawed assumptions about the conflict.
The piece likens Trump’s missteps to George Constanza’s self‑deprecating quote, suggesting every strategic choice on Iran has produced unintended, disastrous outcomes.

items.subject: Roy Cooper’s Radical Strategy: Act Normal
bullets: Polls show former governor Roy Cooper leading Republican Michael Whatley by nine points in the NC Senate race, despite his low‑key, “Make Stuff Cost Less” campaign focused on utility and grocery costs.

Democratic pollster John Anzalone argues Cooper’s authentic, folksy appeal resonates with independents and frustrated voters, a strategy that helped him win tight statewide races like the 2016 governor’s race.

North Carolina’s narrow presidential margins (Trump +1.3‑3.7 points, Romney +2.0) suggest the state remains competitive, but Democrats must still win unaffiliated voters and a slice of rural Trump support to flip the Senate seat.

items.subject: Answering your most burning questions
bullets: The author recounts growing up on a farm, describing rural childhood experiences and how they shaped his perspective.
He addresses readers' curiosity about his personal habits, including his stance on diet soda consumption.
He invites further questions from the audience, encouraging comments for additional insight.

items.subject: Trump’s Crypto Corruption Is Off The Charts — Mehdi and Ben McKenzie Explore Why
bullets: Ben McKenzie’s documentary “Everyone Is Lying to You For Money” streams online from Aug 22 to Sept 6, exposing fraud in the crypto industry and featuring his interview with convicted grifter Sam Bankman‑Fried.
The film traces crypto money flows from Miami to El Salvador to London and argues the industry has deep ties to both Republican and Democratic parties, using the Trump family as a prime fraud target.
Ben bluntly tells disillusioned Democrats to quit the party, warning that corporate crypto interests now dominate its agenda.

items.subject: Exclusive Offer: 50% Off The Lever!
bullets: The Lever, an award‑winning investigative newsroom, reports that oligarch‑funded party insiders are spending millions to protect their preferred candidates in the upcoming midterms, targeting newcomers like Zohran Mamdani, Abdul El‑Sayed, and Melat Kiros.

Zeteo subscribers can get a forever 50% discount on Lever membership—under $1 a week—for full access to investigative reports, newsletters, podcasts, live events, and bonus content such as the ‘Master Plan’ podcast series and a discounted e‑book on legalizing corruption.

The new season of Lever’s ‘Master Plan’ podcast examines the decades‑long effort to create an all‑powerful presidency, culminating in the Trump administration, with early access and extra materials for paid subscribers.

items.subject: Little-Known Episode Offers a Big Clue to El-Sayed’s Politics
bullets: Abdul El‑Sayed publicly backs “Medicare for All” but says he’ll support incremental steps, a public option, and permits employers and unions to keep private plans, though details are vague.

His lack of legislative record as a former city and county health director makes his future Senate stance uncertain, but a little‑known past episode may reveal how he balances reducing corporate power with expanding public coverage.

items.subject: Debt and Tax Cuts
bullets: Krugman argues that the headline $40 trillion debt figure is misleading; measured properly the debt is about $32 trillion and not an immediate crisis despite higher rates.
He blames Republican tax cuts—under George W. Bush and Donald Trump—for inflating the debt-to-GDP ratio, noting that without those cuts the debt would be far lower.
The upcoming installment will propose Democratic policy solutions and examine historical spending, the loss of the Clinton surplus, aging entitlements, and tax‑cut impacts.

items.subject: Marginal Rations
bullets: The diesel crack spread in the US hit a record $102 per barrel, reflecting unprecedented tightness caused by the Ukraine and Iran wars disrupting supply.
Diesel shortages threaten global supply chains because diesel engines power food harvesting and long‑distance freight, risking product shortages and inflation amid Western fiscal crises.
The author warns that hype obscures root causes, urging data‑driven analysis to anticipate government and market responses to the diesel shock.

items.subject: This isn’t my first rodeo
bullets: Roy Cooper claims he has never lost an election, citing six statewide victories in North Carolina and framing the current Senate race as a pivotal fight for Democratic control of the Senate.

He accuses the GOP, President Trump, JD Vance, and far‑right groups of launching a $100 million attack campaign, citing a new poll that ties the race and alleging the attacks are designed to prevent Democrats from regaining the Senate.
Cooper urges supporters to donate $5 to counter the GOP attacks and flip North Carolina blue, linking to a fundraising page for the campaign.

items.subject: This Week in Palestine: Israel Kills At Least 17 Palestinians in Gaza in Days After Kushner Meeting
bullets: An Israeli strike on a Gaza City seaside cafe killed at least six people, including a child, left bodies mangled and forced survivors into the sea, according to eyewitnesses.

The attack occurred a day after Jared Kushner left the region without securing a ceasefire, and Israeli officials reportedly agreed they could continue ‘targeted’ strikes despite the failed negotiations.
In the West Bank, Israeli settlers intensified a siege of Qusra, pledged to return to Gaza, and a Palestinian teen was killed in a settler raid in Khirbet Hamroush.

items.subject: ICE Wants a Weapon That Leaves No Mark
bullets: ICE plans to spend $10‑$20 million on 12,000+ “G.L.O.V.E.” electric‑shock gloves from Compliant Technologies, marketing them as non‑lethal de‑escalation tools but critics say they’re meant to avoid video evidence and lawsuits

The gloves are classified as “hard techniques” in ICE’s force continuum, allowed only when empty‑handed methods fail, yet the manufacturer warns they must not be used on vulnerable groups and limits shocks to 15 seconds, a rule ICE’s training may ignore

A Kentucky lawsuit alleges a detainee was shocked dozens of times, with some shocks lasting up to 99 seconds, highlighting the risk of misuse despite required certification that ICE has yet to fully adopt

items.subject: “Slowing down sounds admirable until you realize that most of slowness is just being bored and alone in your thoug…
bullets: Katie Lowe marks two years of an analog, phone‑free experiment, describing evenings of quiet gardening, chores and long phone‑free conversations as a new normal that feels both soothing and anxiety‑provoking.

Natasha Stagg argues that contemporary writers are pressured to become influencers, noting how literary success is now measured by algorithms, cash prizes with demanding promotional duties, and the uneasy need for agents to shield them from relentless marketing tasks.

The newsletter links to longer pieces on Lowe’s slow‑life experiment and Stagg’s critique of the literary market, inviting readers to explore the full arguments behind these personal and industry reflections.

items.subject: A Federal Judge Is Promoting His Pro-Israel Book Live From His Judicial Chambers
bullets: Judge Roy Altman, a Trump‑appointed Southern District of Florida judge, has livestreamed from his chambers on pro‑Israel shows, labeling the Palestinian keffiyeh a “terrorism scarf” and promoting his book denying genocide.

Altman has joined right‑wing groups claiming to fight “lawful Islamism,” bragged about taking 10% of the federal judiciary on trips to Israel, and allegedly used judicial trips to shape other judges’ views on Israel and Gaza.
A Florida attorney has filed a complaint with the U.S. Court of Appeals alleging Altman violated judicial ethics for his public political activities and use of judicial resources.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: The 2028 Electability Trap Roiling Democrats
bullets: Dan Pfeiffer argues that the 2028 Democratic electability debate is driven by a myth of swing‑voter bias, limiting candidate choices and lowering the party’s ceiling.

He cites Kamala Harris’s 2024 loss in swing states and the Georgia governor race, where Keisha Lance Bottoms won most counties, to show that perceived electability often misjudges real voter behavior.
Pfeiffer warns that this discourse can trap Democrats in a cycle of self‑imposed constraints, preventing diverse and potentially winning candidates from emerging.

items.subject: A Wild Week: Human Printers, Ossoff, Todd Blanche, Baseball and so much more
bullets: ICE arrested Haitian pastor Carl Ruby in Springfield, targeting 30 people in a Cincinnati ICE jail, prompting calls to support Haitian Community Help & Support Center, St. Vincent de Paul, and Second Harvest Food Bank.
The Bulwark plans a fall tour with live shows in Columbia, Charlotte, Atlanta, and a book tour for Sarah’s new book “How to Eat an Elephant,” encouraging subscribers to join events and chat groups.
A new game, YEA or NAY, lets players test historical Senate voting patterns, highlighting how rare perfect party‑line votes are and offering a trivia‑style challenge for political enthusiasts.

items.subject: Jared Bernstein on Debt
bullets: Bernstein warns that the U.S. debt trajectory has turned risky as the growth rate (≈2% real) now roughly matches or falls below interest rates, while the deficit runs about 6% of GDP, double the sustainable level he argues for.

He attributes the worsening fiscal outlook primarily to the permanent Bush and Trump tax cuts, which he and Bobby Kogan estimate would have kept the debt‑to‑GDP ratio stable if omitted, and notes that Democrats helped cement these cuts.
Bernstein says CBO’s optimistic debt forecasts rely on continued tariff revenues and fading Trump cuts—assumptions that appear unrealistic, making the current budget math far less comfortable.

items.subject: Jon Ossoff is Winning the Voters Democrats Need Most (with Amy Walter)
bullets: Sen. Jon Ossoff is gaining traction among Georgia swing voters, according to a recent focus group that highlighted his appeal over his opponent; Amy Walter and Sarah Longwell analyze why Ossoff resonates with undecided voters.

The podcast examines the massive polling errors in Wisconsin and Michigan primaries, featuring a Wisconsin focus group that explains how David Crowley’s last‑minute surge was possible despite earlier misreadings.
They discuss AOC’s “Woke 1 was crazy” remarks and explore whether swing voters’ complaints about both parties stem from politicians’ actions or broader cultural influences.

items.subject: This Week in Democracy – Week 83: Supreme Court Hands Trump Ballroom Victory as He Pushes More Fake Noncitizen Vot…
bullets: Attorney General Todd Blanche refused to pledge DOJ independence and hinted the department may ask the Supreme Court to overturn dozens of lost lawsuits seeking voter‑roll data.
The DOJ announced plans to deploy roughly 1,000 election monitors for the November midterms, despite evidence that voter fraud is virtually nonexistent.

The Supreme Court temporarily blocked a lower‑court order, allowing construction of the White House ballroom to continue, with the project now two‑thirds complete and a 250‑person crew working around the clock.

items.subject: George Conway: For Trump, Harp Strikes a Chord
bullets: Natalie Harp’s newly released love notes to Trump reveal obsessive devotion and suggest an abusive dynamic centered on feeding his fragile ego with flattering stories
George Conway joins Tim Miller on the weekend podcast to argue Trump is governing like a socialist, inflating national debt and meddling in the midterms, confirming the ‘orange man bad’ narrative
Michael Cohen is highlighted as a pathetic lapdog while the newsletter promotes upcoming Bulwark LIVE events and additional podcast content

bullets: Defending the Bonds

items.subject: ‘Tony’ Review
bullets: Matt Johnson’s biopic “Tony” portrays a young Anthony Bourdain’s redemption through hard work and honesty, framing his lies as original sin and his eventual truth‑telling as grace.
The film leans on classic biopic beats but stands out with strong performances from Dominic Sessa, Antonio Banderas as the mentor Chef, and Leo Woodall as the intense line cook.
While the author remains skeptical of Bourdain’s cult status, they praise “Tony” as a well‑crafted, high‑level entry that pierces the mythic image of the chef‑author.

items.subject: Is Jon Ossoff the One We’ve Been Waiting For?
bullets: The show featured Sen. Darlene Graham claiming South Carolina voters prioritize the boys‑vs‑girls sports issue over Taiwan, despite there being no boys playing girls’ sports in the state.

Former CIA analyst Julia Curlee, who served under Trump, Biden, and Trump again, was dismissed after MAGA influencers exposed her as trans, raising questions about civil servant loyalty to an elected Trump.
The episode teased a discussion on whether Jon Ossoff is the key Democratic figure, introduced a new 'Pickleball talk' segment, and promoted the members‑only Secret Podcast.

items.subject: Here’s a Blueprint for What Democrats Should Do If They Take Back the House
bullets: Alex Jones warned on X that a Trump‑initiated war in Iran could lead to a draft and total war, urging Democrats to act to stop Trump’s “tyranny.”

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Democrats aren’t focusing on impeachment now, but a post‑election Democratic win would demand immediate accountability as Trump’s approval sits at 33% with 73% saying he ignores key problems.

The newsletter argues that without restoring constitutional rule of law, any Democratic policy agenda—like tackling the affordability crisis—will be moot, calling for “Nuremberg‑style” actions against Trump’s alleged illegal conduct.

items.subject: We’re in for a long race
bullets: Vice President and President Trump have targeted Gov. Roy Cooper in North Carolina, warning that a Republican win in the state could secure GOP Senate control until 2029.
Cooper’s campaign faces heavy attacks from Trump’s allies, including Stephen Miller, and stresses the need for fundraising to fund ads and counter the GOP’s messaging.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Your New Senator Is a Total Lightweight. She’s Perfect.
bullets: Darline Graham, South Carolina senator and Lindsey Graham’s sister, stumbled over a Taiwan question in a debate, claiming foreign policy isn’t her expertise while her brother has long championed U.S. support for Taiwan.

The author notes that none of eleven GOP Senate China hawks—Jim Risch, Tom Cotton, Josh Hawley, Pete Ricketts, Dan Sullivan, Todd Young, Bill Hagerty, Marsha Blackburn, Rick Scott, John Cornyn, and Ted Cruz—responded to a request for comments on Trump’s abrupt cut of joint U.S.–South Korea exercises, highlighting a perceived lack of engagement on China policy.

The piece argues that many GOP senators prioritize culture‑war issues over substantive foreign‑policy debate, suggesting that voters may be more concerned with domestic partisan battles than with strategic challenges like the South China Sea and U.S. alliances.

items.subject: ⬇️ Trump Advisers Worry He Could ‘Sink to the High 20s’
bullets: Reuters/Ipsos and Fox News polls show Trump’s approval has fallen to a historic low of 33% ahead of the midterms, with private GOP‑commissioned polls hovering around 30%‑35%.

A Financial Times survey finds nearly 25% of 2024 Trump voters say they are financially worse off since his return to office, while Republican strategists fear his war on Iran will further depress GOP turnout in crucial midterms.
Michael Cohen, once a Trump critic, returned to interview the president on his radio show, highlighting internal GOP anxiety about Trump potentially sinking into the low‑20% approval range.

items.subject: Trump Just Ordered the Government to Delete the Receipts (w/ Andrew Weissmann)
bullets: Trump ordered the federal government to delete corporate ownership records, a move that could obscure financial ties and raise legal questions about record‑keeping transparency.
Weissmann explains the latest Fauci investigation, noting new evidence that could impact the probe’s scope and potential charges.

An Alaska election controversy involving a disputed absentee ballot led to a DOJ investigation, highlighting vulnerabilities in election security and the administration’s handling of contested results.

items.subject: Scott Bessent Fails to Gaslight the Market
bullets: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a Trump loyalist, pushed a controversial plan to put Trump’s signature on U.S. currency and denied a K‑shaped economy despite data showing widening inequality, eroding market credibility.

Nearly half of Trump‑appointed top Treasury officials have quit, many citing illegal demands such as a $1.8 billion “anti‑weaponization” fund and misuse of taxpayer data, highlighting internal turmoil.

Bessent’s recent 30‑year Treasury bond buyback, funded by short‑term debt, mirrors quantitative easing in an inflationary environment, briefly lowered yields but quickly rebounded, underscoring the futility of his politically‑driven market intervention.

items.subject: Trump’s War on Reality Comes for the Census
bullets: The author now warns that the Trump administration has infiltrated the U.S. Census Bureau, compromising its traditionally nonpartisan data collection.
Because of this interference, the author can no longer trust any federal statistical releases, including unemployment and inflation figures.
The detailed story explaining the infiltration is behind a paywall, accessible with a Bulwark+ membership.

items.subject: He Co-Founded Airbnb. Now He’s a Red-Pilled Billionaire Helping Trump
bullets: Joe Gebbia, Airbnb co‑founder, donated $200k to both Hillary Clinton’s 2016 campaign and Joe Biden’s 2020 campaign before abandoning the Democrats in 2024 and now publicly backs Trump, RFK Jr, and Elon Musk while sharing extremist, COVID‑denial, and election‑fraud content on X.

Recent X activity shows Gebbia amplifying far‑right narratives, including a John Birch Society post blaming illegal immigration for housing prices, a claim that NGOs manipulate migrants, and a false headline that Los Angeles would let non‑citizens vote.

Gebbia, now the U.S. government’s first chief design officer, uses his platform to spread white‑supremacist rhetoric and conspiracy theories, linking Democratic policies to alleged election fraud and praising radical right‑wing financiers like Bill Ackman.

items.subject: Trump Is Finally Losing Ground Among Republicans
bullets: Recent focus groups of straight‑ticket Republicans show a noticeable shift, with many now grading Trump a C or D rather than the usual A‑B ratings.

The author notes that while earlier supporters praised Trump’s promises and personal finance impact, current sentiment reflects disappointment and deflation among voters who previously backed him three times.
These findings suggest a growing willingness among some GOP voters to sit out the midterms or even consider non‑Trump options.

items.subject: The Dollar, the Dopamine, and JD Vance
bullets: JD Vance, once a MAGA think‑tank speaker, blamed Silicon Valley Bank’s failure on “woke idiots” and argued that zero‑interest policy created a subsidy for finance and tech, while also claiming the dollar’s reserve status is a “resource curse” that cheapens US debt, a stance the author says aligns with his support for the Iran war and de‑dollarization efforts

The newsletter highlights a Venezuelan family legally in the US who were arrested during a self‑deportation attempt and now sit in a Texas ICE facility, urging readers to contact Senator Katie Britt for assistance

It introduces “limbic capitalism,” a concept from David Courtwright’s *Age of Addiction* linking brain‑reward systems to market practices that exploit addictive behaviors across industries like gambling, alcohol, and tech

items.subject: Israel Finally Admits to Killing Hind Rajab. 933 Days Later
bullets: Israel officially acknowledged, 933 days after the incident, that its soldiers fired on Hind Rajab’s vehicle, killing the 5‑year‑old and her relatives, after years of denial backed by the U.S. State Department.

Prem Thakker’s video critiques U.S. officials for feigning concern while deferring to Israel’s self‑investigation, and notes the killing occurred alongside the deaths of medics and is part of over 73,000 Palestinian deaths, including 20,000 children.

items.subject: The Iran War Is Eating the GOP’s Midterm Message Alive
bullets: House Republicans are scrambling to explain rising gas and grocery prices caused by the Iran war, with Speaker Mike Johnson blaming the conflict while claiming tax cuts had boosted the economy in Q1 2024.

Republican leaders, including Johnson, Tom Emmer, and Steve Scalise, repeatedly justify the war as necessary to stop Iran’s nuclear progress, yet President Trump has publicly downplayed the threat, calling the war gratuitous.

The GOP struggles to reconcile their narrative of American energy dominance and control of the Strait of Hormuz with evidence that Iranian drones and missiles continue to disrupt tanker traffic, undermining their messaging to swing‑district voters.

items.subject: Affordable housing should be within reach
bullets: North Carolina’s housing crisis is driven by soaring rents, high gas costs, and corporate landlords; Gov. Cooper pledges to cut red tape, ban algorithm‑driven rent hikes, and restrict large‑portfolio buyers to lower prices.

Cooper highlights past successes—hundreds of millions in mortgage relief, $355 million in community grants, and vetoing bills that hurt low‑income renters—while urging federal action to roll back Trump tariffs on lumber, steel, and aluminum.

He calls for faster, smarter construction (multi‑family and modular homes) and modernized permitting to increase supply, aiming to make home ownership and renting affordable for working families across the state.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Politicians Suddenly Notice Everybody Hates Data Centers
bullets: Texas Gov. Greg Abbott halted up to 1,800 data‑center projects and signed a moratorium pending an energy‑use audit, while Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro added red‑tape to new data‑center proposals.

In Ohio, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned that Sen. Jon Husted’s support for AI data centers could cost him the seat, with Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown using the issue as a campaign centerpiece.

Michigan’s Green Party nominated 25‑year‑old Shane Dedrick via a Zoom convention, but he has no campaign presence, has not registered with the FEC, and the party has since stopped promoting him on social media.

items.subject: 🦅 🇮🇷 Yep, Iran’s Definitely ‘Cartering’ Trump
bullets: Mike Lindell, a top Trump‑backed election‑fraud donor, refuses to concede his Minnesota GOP primary loss and is pushing a private recount plan to replace electronic voting machines, echoing the GOP’s broader anti‑vote‑machine stance.

U.S. intelligence officials warned that Iran’s war strategy is deliberately dragging on to “Carter” Trump—using prolonged conflict to erode his popularity and hurt Republicans in the 2024 election, a view now confirmed as the war shows no end in sight.

The article links the ongoing, unpopular war, rising gas prices, and a looming global economic downturn to the Trump‑Vance administration’s inability to admit defeat, warning of severe political and economic fallout.

items.subject: The Case Against Bond Market Panic
bullets: Krugman argues that despite the U.S. debt reaching $40 trillion, borrowing in its own currency makes a Greek‑style crisis implausible, and market data show little fear of default.
He warns Democrats not to repeat Obama‑era scaremongering by “Very Serious People” who use debt panic to force austerity, urging progressive tax reforms instead.
While acknowledging fiscal irresponsibility under Trump, Krugman says debt panic is unwarranted and would hinder future Democratic policy goals.

items.subject: Is the Media Afraid of Covering the Natalie Harp-Donald Trump Dynamic?
bullets: Journalism ethics scholars Eric Deggans and Subbu Vincent debate whether probing aide Natalie Harp’s personal letters to Donald Trump—described as “all that matters to” him and alarming the Secret Service—is fair game after Sen. Jon Ossoff highlighted her in a campaign speech.

The piece notes that MS NOW’s Katy Tur abruptly shifted away from the Harp story, underscoring media hesitation, while Disney is praised for opposing Trump despite earlier actions that helped fuel his anti‑media stance.

items.subject: GOP Iowa Nominee’s Million-Dollar Sex-Toy Problem
bullets: Zach Lahn, Iowa GOP gubernatorial candidate, invested $1 million in FirmTech in 2021, becoming its second‑largest shareholder with a 28.2 % stake and later retained 25 % ownership through an LLC.
FirmTech, marketed as a medical device company, sold “erection rings” and a clitoral vibrator that were described as sex toys, contradicting Lahn’s claim that he only supported therapeutic products.

Lahn resigned from FirmTech’s board in September 2023 before any pleasure products were released, yet SEC filings show he owned shares and signed documents promoting those very products during his tenure.

items.subject: The Silence of Western Feminists Over Gaza Exposes Their Fraud
bullets: Miscarriages in Gaza have tripled in the first half of the year, rising to nearly 4,000 cases, a figure that has not sparked global feminist activism despite similar reactions to other women's rights issues.

items.subject: Trump’s Human Printer Is Cray-Cray
bullets: The Bulwark’s upcoming Good Fight Tour hits the Southeast in October, with tickets on sale Aug 21 and early presale for Bulwark+ members.
Trump’s 32‑year‑old aide Natalie Harp serves as his “human printer,” lugging a portable printer, paper and batteries to feed the president printed briefs.
The newsletter notes the story was first reported by Marc Caputo in May 2024, highlighting the bizarre nature of Trump’s reliance on printed memos.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: Why Every 2028 Campaign Should Study Angie Nixon's Win
bullets: Angie Nixon, a Florida state rep, defeated heavily funded national security official Alex Vindman in the Democratic primary by over 11 points, despite a spending gap of more than 10‑to‑1.
The upset signals a shift away from establishment-backed candidates, showing grassroots, under‑funded contenders can win against well‑known, financially advantaged opponents.
Pfeiffer argues 2028 Democratic campaigns should study Nixon’s strategy—leveraging local credibility and voter dissatisfaction—to replicate her outsider victory.

items.subject: TODAY, 4PM ET: Francesca Albanese Joins Mehdi for a Live Town Hall Q&A
bullets: Settler violence in the occupied West Bank has reached an all‑time high, with extremist settlers besieging homes in Qusra, cutting off electricity and water, and attacking municipal workers.
Israel’s national security minister has publicly called for nightly “targeted assassinations” of 30‑40 people in Gaza, amid the ongoing genocide.
UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese, a vocal critic of Netanyahu, will join Mehdi for a live Zeteo town‑hall at 4 PM ET to discuss the West Bank “pogroms” and Gaza crisis.

items.subject: When wildfire smoke hits home
bullets: Wildfire smoke exposure is rising nationwide, with climate models predicting larger, more frequent fires and smoke reaching far‑away states like Florida; indoor AQI can be 60% of outdoor levels without filtration.

A 2025 review of 33 studies found N95 masks filter up to 94% of PM2.5, yet were underused; firefighters only got voluntary N95 permission in 2025, despite 8‑43% higher lung‑cancer risk and 16‑30% higher cardiovascular death risk.

To protect health, wear a fitted N95 when AQI hits 150 (or 100 for sensitive groups) and upgrade home filtration to MERV‑13 or HEPA with continuous operation, aiming for indoor/outdoor ratios below 20% and a clean‑air refuge room.

items.newsletter: Here Be Dragons from Barbara F. Walter
items.subject: Trump Just Told the World: Get the Bomb
bullets: Trump’s threats to withdraw U.S. extended deterrence for NATO, Japan, South Korea and his cuts to joint exercises push allies toward developing their own nuclear arsenals.
By tearing up the Iran nuclear deal and befriending Kim Jong‑un, Trump incentivizes adversaries like Iran and North Korea to pursue bombs, increasing proliferation risks.
More nuclear states raise the chance of accidents or deliberate use, undermining the non‑proliferation stability the U.S. historically secured through guarantees and sanctions.

items.subject: Polling, War, Harvey Lee West
bullets: Cooper says Trump’s war in Iran is draining gas, grocery and utility costs and lacks any clear strategy, fueling voter frustration in North Carolina.

He warns that Republican opponent Michael Whatley, former NC GOP chair, appointed convicted child molester Harvey Lee West to a leadership role to raise money, prompting a party resolution to bar such appointments.

Cooper claims he leads in polls, faces $100 million in Republican ads, and urges donations and volunteer support to win the open Senate seat and address cost‑of‑living, health care, and democratic checks.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Disney Says No to the Lyin’ King
bullets: Sen. Darline Graham, a new Republican senator from South Carolina, admitted in a GOP primary debate that she is not knowledgeable about national security issues like Taiwan and the South China Sea, though she supports the military.

Disney/ABC’s parent companies, Paramount and ABC, settled for $16 million and $16 million respectively in lawsuits involving Donald Trump’s claims over a 60 Minutes interview and the E. Jean Carroll case, despite the cases being largely meritless and the settlements dwarfing the companies’ revenues.

items.subject: 👱‍♀️ 🖨️ Inside Trumpland’s Freakout Over ‘Natalie’
bullets: Trump ordered a sweeping leak‑hunt after Natalie Harp’s private letters were published, calling the leak an “invasion of privacy” and demanding phone inspections from suspected moles.

The political fallout saw Republicans and Trump‑aligned officials mobilize to defend Harp, treating her as a protected asset and sparking a cult‑ish defense of her honor across the GOP and federal apparatus.
Meanwhile, progressives won a surprising upset in Florida and the Trump administration continued to target the International Criminal Court, highlighting ongoing geopolitical tensions.

items.subject: What Are Bond Markets Telling Us?
bullets: Long‑term government bond yields have spiked to mid‑2000s levels because soaring credit demand—from AI‑driven datacenter investment and massive U.S. deficits after Trump’s tax cuts—outpaces supply, not because of solvency fears.

Krugman argues there’s no evidence of a looming U.S. debt crisis: inflation breakeven rates and credit‑default swap spreads remain flat, and countries borrowing in their own currency rarely run out of money.

He urges future Democratic policymakers not to panic, to avoid the 2009‑10 debt‑scare narrative, and to eventually address deficits, but stresses the current rate rise is a credit‑demand issue, not a crisis.

items.subject: Pro-Israel Groups Want You to Believe That Israel’s National Security Minister… Doesn’t Represent Israel
bullets: Israel’s national security minister Itamar Ben‑Gvir called on a podcast to kill 30‑40 Palestinians nightly, saying many “shouldn’t live” and are “not even people.”
U.S. pro‑Israel groups condemned Ben‑Gvir, claiming he doesn’t represent Israeli policy, despite his role as the top security official and Israel’s ongoing Gaza campaign since Oct 7.
Ben‑Gvir also advocated forced expulsion of Gaza’s residents and settlement of the strip, urging emigration for civilians while promising to kill “terrorists” one by one.

items.subject: Make Measles Great Again
bullets: National kindergarten exemption rates rose to 4.2% in 2025‑26, up from 3.6% the year before, with Idaho topping the chart at 17% and MMR coverage as low as 75% there.

Measles cases have exceeded 2,500 this year—the highest in 35 years—driven by pockets of communities below the 95% herd‑immunity threshold, while pertussis remains above pre‑pandemic levels and vitamin‑K refusals have caused infant deaths.

The Trump administration’s new executive order directs agencies, including the Justice Department, to pressure states that make vaccine exemptions hard to obtain, signaling a federal push to loosen school‑vaccination requirements.

items.newsletter: Tim, Sarah and JVL - The Bulwark
items.subject: Melania May Be Behind MAGA’s Natalie Harp Freakout
bullets: Former Trump voter recounts seeing a loved one affected by immigration policies he supported, highlighting the personal cost of his political choices.
Sen. Jon Ossoff’s claim that Trump and Natalie Harp frequently travel together sparks a faux outrage in MAGA circles, exposing intra‑party tensions.
Florida’s primary is poised to become competitive in the fall, while Pete Hegseth’s Iowa trip raises questions about his candidacy and the state’s influence on the GOP race.

items.subject: The Death of Mainstream Media? Ex-CNN and CBS Journalists Weigh In
bullets: He warns that the Washington Post’s financial instability poses a greater threat to democratic discourse than owner Jeff Bezos’s right‑wing politics

items.subject: Between stops: A few of the books I’ve enjoyed
bullets: Cooper notes North Carolina voters are feeling high grocery, gas, and health‑care costs, and he frames his Senate bid as a fight for affordable health care and working‑family protections

items.subject: The Cruelty Was Fine Until It Became Personal
bullets: Brent Jindra, a three‑time Trump voter and tech salesman, married Russian immigrant Galina Bobreneva, who was detained after a domestic flight and placed in a Mojave desert internment camp despite not crossing a border.
The author uses the case to illustrate the hypocrisy of anti‑immigrant rhetoric, highlighting how policies that target “bad” immigrants can turn personal and brutal when applied to ordinary families.
The piece serves as a warning that cruelty justified by ideology becomes starkly visible when it affects individuals like Brent and Galina.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: How America Ends Up Alone
bullets: Wisconsin GOP Gov. candidate Tom Tiffany, who backed Trump’s 2020 election‑overturn efforts, now publicly concedes Biden won and pledges to certify future Wisconsin results, illustrating GOP pivot for electability.
Former President Trump threatened to bomb Oman after it engaged with Iran over the Strait of Hormuz, despite a 40‑year U.S. partnership that provides strategic ports and diplomatic channels.

The author warns that such erratic moves—threatening allies, cutting joint exercises, praising adversaries—erode trust, risk alienating partners like South Korea, Japan and Gulf states, and could leave America isolated.

items.subject: EXCLUSIVE: Voters Oppose Netanyahu-Led Scheme to Integrate U.S. and Israeli Militaries
bullets: A new Demand Progress/IMEU/DFP poll shows a majority of U.S. voters oppose Section 219, a bipartisan proposal to merge U.S. and Israeli militaries, and believe Israel gains more from the current aid regime.

The poll, released by Zeteo, indicates voters support lawmakers who voted to cut U.S. aid to Israel in a recent House vote, reflecting widespread skepticism of deepening U.S. military integration with Israel.

items.subject: A New Level of Trumpian Evil
bullets: Trump’s shift toward a “very good relationship with Kim Jong Un” betrays South Korea, a democratic success story that rose from war poverty to a Western‑level standard of living and a major semiconductor supplier.

South Korea’s robust military budget, comparable to Ukraine’s, and its status as a key U.S. ally underscore the strategic loss when Trump undermines a nation that defended American interests during the Korean War.
Krugman argues that Trump’s preference for a totalitarian regime over a functioning democracy signals a fundamental rejection of the values that underpin U.S. foreign policy and national identity.

items.subject: Covid-19 and dengue creeping up, vaccinations creeping down, a new mRNA flu vaccine, and more
bullets: Covid-19 cases are rising nationwide, with the South and West leading; the CDC expects 10‑15% of the population to be infected this wave and urges high‑risk groups to get vaccinated now

The first US locally transmitted dengue case was identified in Virginia, signaling that warmer seasons and infected travelers may make such mosquito‑borne illnesses increasingly common, though outbreaks remain unlikely

Moderna’s mRNA flu shot (mFlusiva) showed 27% higher efficacy than standard flu vaccines in adults 50+, but causes more injection‑site pain, fatigue and headaches; it should be available to those 65+ on Medicare this fall, while broader rollout for 50‑64 remains uncertain

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: Trump Is Giving Your Money to His Corporate Backers
bullets: Trump's tariffs cost the average American family $1,100 annually, were deemed unconstitutional and later struck down by the Supreme Court, yet the $166 billion collected was refunded to corporations like Apple ($2 bn), Amazon ($600 m) and potentially Walmart ($10 bn).
Polls show strong voter backlash: about 60% disapprove of the tariffs, 72% believe they raised prices, and 78% think any refunds should go to consumers rather than corporations.
The newsletter urges Democrats to spotlight this issue as a clear example of Trump harming consumers while rewarding corporate donors, framing it as a winning election talking point.

items.subject: Over Target
bullets: Chevron secured a lucrative joint‑venture in Kazakhstan’s Tengiz‑Korolev field in April 1993, helping double Kazakh oil output to 2 million bpd by 2025.

The Caspian Pipeline Consortium, carrying ~1.4 million bpd of Kazakh crude to Russia’s Black Sea port Novorossiysk, was halted after Ukrainian drone attacks damaged a mooring on Nov 29, prompting a rare U.S. State Department protest to Kyiv.
The author warns that these attacks signal a broader threat to Western energy interests and suggest the Ukraine war cannot be contained, foreshadowing deeper conflict over Black Sea supply routes.

items.subject: A 7-Year-Old Trapped in Hell Is Begging Senator Katie Britt for Help
bullets: A Venezuelan family—pregnant mother, father, and their 7‑year‑old daughter—who complied with every immigration requirement, including asylum application, ICE check‑ins, and self‑deportation, have been held for weeks at Texas’s Dilley detention center instead of being returned to Venezuela.
The author urges readers to call Senator Katie Britt at 202‑224‑5744 to intervene on the family’s behalf, highlighting the case as an example of the Trump‑era immigration system’s failures.

items.subject: Who is Natalie Harp? The Trump Aide Dominating the Headlines Right Now
bullets: Senator Jon Ossoff mocked Trump’s alleged plan to travel with aide Natalie Harp on a Qatar‑gifted “flying palace,” sparking widespread curiosity about her role.
Natalie Harp, dubbed Trump’s “human binkie” by NYT’s Maggie Haberman, was reportedly on a catering truck that helped Trump switch planes in Turkey amid a claimed Iranian assassination threat.
The newsletter lists seven key facts about Harp, highlighting her close access to Trump, including her presence on the decoy flight and her rapid rise within the inner circle.

items.subject: SCOOP: Trump’s Iran War Has Burned Through Well Over 90% of Key Long-Range Missiles
bullets: Zeteo reports that the U.S. war in Iran has exhausted well over 90% of its crucial long‑range missile stockpiles since February.
President Trump has labeled journalists exposing the depletion as “treason” and has directed the Justice Department to aggressively investigate and hunt down leakers.
The newsletter argues the weapons shortage and press‑crackdown illustrate how disastrous the Iran conflict has become for the United States.

items.subject: An update on the ground
bullets: The campaign reports that volunteers have knocked on 215,000 doors, called 440,000 voters, and recruited over 16,000 volunteers as the North Carolina Senate race approaches its two‑month deadline.

Roy Cooper highlights his record expanding Medicaid to hundreds of thousands, protecting families as Attorney General, and now seeks a U.S. Senate seat, urging donations and voter registration ahead of the upcoming vote.

items.subject: Is the DSA a Republican Psy-Op?
bullets: Hakeem Jeffries told reporters he does not support the Democratic Socialists of America’s agenda, emphasizing he is a Democrat, not a DSA member.

The author argues the DSA’s national organization is a “false‑flag” operation allegedly run by the Heritage Foundation to sabotage the Democratic Party, suggesting its leaders may be covert moderates like Mamdani.

items.subject: Don’t Let Them Fool You: You are Not Alone
bullets: Pete Buttigieg argues that labels like “red” oversimplify communities, citing Indiana’s 2008 Obama win and 2023 bipartisan resistance to Trump‑Vance gerrymandering as proof of dynamic political change.
He claims a growing American majority is ready for reform, urging viewers to join a coalition that could win in the next 80 days, and invites comments on his new video.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Trump ‘Won’ on Tariffs? Lol.
bullets: Trump’s tariffs, though widely criticized for harming growth, prices, and manufacturing, have not triggered a global economic collapse, with markets largely shrugging off their impact amid AI‑driven growth and a stalled Iran war.

Politico’s claim that Trump “won” on tariffs rests on the fact that the most extreme tariffs were abandoned after bond‑market panic and that tech firms importing AI infrastructure largely escaped tariffs, masking broader economic damage.

The newsletter argues that praising Trump for avoiding catastrophic tariffs is misleading, as the remaining tariffs still hurt the economy while the AI boom and Iran conflict divert attention from these blunders.

items.subject: Is a New, Expanded Progressive 'Squad' Coming to Congress in 2027?
bullets: Justice Democrats endorsed four progressive House primary winners—Darializa Avila Chevalier, Claire Valdez, Dr. Adam Hamawy, Donavan McKinney, and Chris Rabb—signaling a potential new progressive bloc for 2027.
Usamah Andrabi argues Democratic voters reject endless wars and want unbought leaders, noting AIPAC’s multi‑million‑dollar spending against pro‑Palestinian candidates influences primaries.
The interview is available in full to paid subscribers, with a three‑minute preview for free readers.

items.subject: 💰 A Bank Closed Trump Accounts for ‘Anti-Money Laundering Reasons.’ So Now He's Giving Himself… a Bank?
bullets: Capital One closed over 300 Trump Organization accounts in early August, citing anti‑money‑laundering concerns, while two weeks later the OCC, led by Trump‑appointed Jonathan Gould, gave conditional preliminary approval for a bank charter to Trump’s crypto firm World Liberty Trust.
Senator Elizabeth Warren called the OCC’s charter approval the “most brazen act of self‑dealing” in U.S. financial history and announced legislation to block such conflicts of interest.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: Thoughts on the Michigan Poll Freaking Out Democrats
bullets: A new Fox News poll shows Republican Mike Rogers leading Democrat Abdul El‑Sayed by four points in the Michigan Senate race, sparking panic among Democrats who once felt confident about the seat.
Pfeiffer argues the poll’s crosstabs and El‑Sayed’s historical performance suggest the lead may be misleading and that the Democrat remains competitive despite concerns about his electability.
He contends that losing Michigan would narrow the Senate path for Democrats, but emphasizes that the poll’s methodology and past trends could still favor El‑Sayed.

items.subject: The Misery Will Continue Until Morale Improves
bullets: Krugman warns that the U.S. military is facing critical shortages, citing depleted precision missiles and dire ship conditions like flooding toilets on the USS Lincoln and lack of basic supplies on the USS Boxer.

He blames Trump’s erratic, aesthetic‑driven directives—such as demanding new “Trump‑class” battleships and retro‑style carrier modifications—for undermining professional logistics and exacerbating the crisis.

Krugman argues the broader problem is an emerging authoritarian dynamic where party officials and the Pentagon ignore bad news, allowing incompetence and ego to dominate policy until press coverage forces action.

items.subject: The DNC’s Summer Pep Rally
bullets: DNC chair Ken Martin used the Austin summer meeting to dismiss criticism and project confidence, while senior Democrats like Donna Brazile and Terry McAuliffe urged unity and warned against internal complaining.
The meeting approved a new 2028 primary calendar—South Carolina first on Jan 22—yet many DNC insiders remain skeptical of Martin’s fundraising, voter‑protection, and primary‑organizing abilities.
Kamala Harris’s PAC mistakenly backed Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola, prompting the campaign to distance itself, highlighting Harris’s limited appeal outside core Democratic states.

items.subject: Help Zeteo Defend Democracy From Trump
bullets: Zeteo’s recent ‘Start The Steal’ series exposed multiple Trump and GOP efforts to subvert the 2024 midterm elections, framing them as a defining moment of American authoritarianism.
A live town hall and an interview with former Trump lawyer Ty Cobb, who warned democracy may not survive Trump’s attacks, garnered coverage in several major news outlets.
Zeteo urges readers to become paid subscribers to fund continued investigative reporting on these election‑subversion activities.

items.subject: How ‘Psychopath’ Trump’s Mayhem Will Backfire in 2028 for Republicans
bullets: Norm Ornstein argues that despite a law barring Trump from the 2028 ballot, GOP figures like Rubio, Cruz, Vance and Burgum stay silent because the party has become a Trump‑centric cult.
He warns that soaring inflation and unaffordable healthcare make any alliance with the failing president politically toxic for Republicans.
Ornstein also blames Newt Gingrich and Mitch McConnell for enabling Trump’s dominance, suggesting they share responsibility for the party’s current crisis.

items.subject: MAGA’s Future Is in Florida (with Will Sommer)
bullets: Will Sommer and Sarah Longwell analyze Florida’s GOP governor primary, noting a Trump‑endorsed ‘MAGA establishment’ candidate, a flamboyantly racist groyper, and a DeSantis‑aligned contender struggling for traction.
They discuss how the race reflects the future of Tucker Carlson’s America First faction and growing dissatisfaction among rank‑and‑file Trump voters.

items.subject: Demography, Deportations and the Trump Stall
bullets: July’s BLS report showed employment fell and earlier months were revised down, confirming economists’ view that the Trump-era job slowdown is a persistent “Trump Stall” rather than a temporary blip.
Krugman attributes the slowdown to two long‑run forces—aging Baby Boomers exiting the labor force and Trump’s harsh crackdown on immigrant workers, which together cut labor‑supply growth.

Fewer workers, especially foreign‑born labor that fills low‑skill jobs, mean lower tax revenues and reduced capacity to fund national security, infrastructure, healthcare, and retirees, harming both short‑ and long‑run American welfare.

items.subject: American Stasi
bullets: The Bulwark is promoting a live comedy show in NYC on Sept 8 with remaining balcony seats and promising a “nuts” surprise if it sells out; Bulwark LIVE tour tickets for SC, NC, and Atlanta go on sale Aug 21 with an exclusive presale for members on Aug 18.

Trump is seeking to have his name placed on the Kennedy Center again, while former DHS agent Karoline Leavitt is moving to the private sector, raising concerns about her misinformation role; JVL highlights a DHS‑linked murder of Alex Pretti that spurred extensive investigations into liberal activist groups in Minnesota.

Sarah’s earlier prediction about the Wisconsin Democratic primary proved correct, and the newsletter teases upcoming commentary on Bernie, AOC, and a members‑only Secret Podcast episode with JVL and Sarah.

items.subject: This Week in Palestine: Israel Shoots 13-Year-Old as She ‘Memorized the Quran’ and Settlers Besiege Palestinian Fa…
bullets: U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee condemned settlers besieging a Palestinian‑American home as “Israeli terrorists” but simultaneously called them “illegal trespassers” and defended most settlers, raising questions about the weight of his rebuke.

This week Israel killed a 13‑year‑old girl allegedly while she was memorizing the Quran, and an Israeli official suggested using Palestinian bodies as bargaining chips, while Netanyahu rejected Donald Trump’s Gaza plan.
The newsletter links multiple recent incidents of settler violence, including attacks in Taybeh and the beating‑to‑death of Palestinian American Sayfollah Musallet, noting a lack of accountability.

items.subject: “At some point in the future, something that is currently considered a high-level skill will be the baseline for e…
bullets: The newsletter argues that high‑level skills (e.g., graphic design, culinary expertise) are becoming baseline expectations, driven by AI tools like ChatGPT and template‑based social media content that erode originality.

It critiques the homogenization of online feeds, noting that Instagram and TikTok reward carousel text‑on‑image formats and unedited, template‑derived videos, leading to a lack of lasting creative impact.

It includes a cultural piece debunking a journalist’s claim that Japanese curry is the worst, tracing seaweed’s 8,000‑year British history and the 1872 Japanese curry adoption to combat vitamin B1 deficiency, and highlighting seaweed’s potential to supply 100 million tonnes of food by the 2040s.

items.subject: Debunking MAGA’s Puppy-Killer Smear Against Abdul El-Sayed
bullets: During Abdul El‑Sayed’s 16‑month tenure as Detroit public health director, the animal‑control “save” rate rose from about 26% in 2015 to roughly 60% in 2016 and approached 70% by 2017, according to animal‑rights expert Melissa Miller.

El‑Sayed inherited a dilapidated, euthanasia‑heavy shelter, appointed Miller as director, and quickly instituted adoption programs and infrastructure fixes that cut euthanasia rates and improved conditions, earning praise from Mayor Mike Duggan.

Right‑wing outlets like the Daily Mail and Fox News spread a false smear claiming El‑Sayed ran a “slaughterhouse,” but the underlying data and interviews show he transformed a dysfunctional department rather than created it.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: How Big Will the Blue Wave Be?
bullets: Dan Pfeiffer questions how many Senate seats Democrats could win in 2024, suggesting a 5‑6 seat gain (e.g., NC, ME, OH, IA, AK, TX) while possibly losing MI; he frames this as a measure of the Blue Wave’s size.

items.subject: 7 Things About Afghanistan the U.S. Wants You to Forget, Five Years After Kabul Fell
bullets: The U.S. evacuated over 120,000 Afghans in August 2021, but hundreds of thousands of promised resettlement cases remain in limbo five years later.
Since the Taliban takeover, women and girls have been systematically excluded from public life, international aid has collapsed, and hunger rates have surged dramatically.
Millions of Afghan refugees have been forced to return, and the country has re‑emerged as a flashpoint for regional conflict despite global attention moving on.

items.subject: Trump to SCOTUS: Make Me
bullets: The newsletter urges readers to volunteer as poll workers, citing Swift’s 2023 article on the nonprofit “Power to the Polls” that recruits volunteers to staff elections amid ongoing shortages.
It highlights a Jay Nordlinger piece questioning whether Donald Trump truly shot a 70‑stroke round of golf, juxtaposing Trump’s self‑promotion with his legal battles over presidential immunity.

items.subject: Vanessa Williamson on Taxes and Democracy
bullets: Williamson argues taxation is the price of democracy because without sufficient revenue governments cannot act on voters’ preferences, a link traced back to Magna Carta’s consent requirement for extraordinary taxes.

She notes that high‑tax, high‑freedom societies (e.g., Nordic countries) contradict anti‑tax myths, while authoritarian regimes keep taxes low by relying on non‑tax revenues like resource rents or fines.

U.S. history shows a shift from a “class tax” on the wealthy and tariff reliance to broad‑based income taxes during WWII, fostering public support for social programs such as Social Security and Medicare.

items.subject: This Week in Democracy – Week 82: A Decoy Plane, ICE’s Electric Gloves, and Government Fascists Investigate the Le…
bullets: The Washington Post revealed Trump used a decoy Air Force One flight, leaving officials like Marco Rubio and Stephen Miller as human shields while he escaped an alleged Iranian assassination threat that U.S. officials could not verify.
ICE plans to spend up to $20 million on electric‑shock gloves for agents, despite manufacturer warnings they not be used on children, pregnant people, or the elderly/disabled.
The Department of Homeland Security launched a sweeping investigation into unrelated left‑wing groups after the killing of Alex Pretti, infiltrating Signal chats and obtaining financial records.

items.subject: ‘The End of Oak Street’ Is the Weirdest Big Movie of the Year
bullets: The End of Oak Street, a $70‑million original starring Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor, thrusts an 1980s suburban family into a Mesozoic nightmare of dinosaurs, delivering a Spielberg‑style, PG‑13 dinosaur chase that critics compare to Jurassic Park and Mitchell’s suspense work in It Follows.

The film’s success highlights a shift toward pricey original movies—like Obsession and Backrooms—amid a domestic box‑office boom, arguing such one‑offs are needed to break the superhero franchise dominance.

In a related industry note, the $50 million theatrical rescue of Coyote vs. Acme after Warner Bros. shelved it illustrates studios’ current strategy of writing off streaming‑first films for tax benefits, prompting indie distributor Ketchup Entertainment to step in.

items.subject: The U.S. Owes Afghanistan a Reckoning – But It Refuses to Have One
bullets: The author argues that Western media has ignored rural Afghanistan, focusing on Kabul’s elite while U.S. drone strikes and death squads devastated villages, fueling radicalization.
He contends the post‑withdrawal narrative paints the U.S. as a benevolent patron betrayed by the Taliban, obscuring the American‑backed violence that enabled the Taliban’s return.

items.subject: ‘A Slaughter in Our Industry’: Home Builders Say ICE is Destroying Their Business
bullets: Vice President Dan Vance blamed an alleged 20 million undocumented immigrants for housing unaffordability, citing a fabricated Federal Reserve “study” that linked immigration to higher home prices.

Contrary to Vance’s claim, ICE enforcement during the first year of Trump’s second term drove new‑home prices up in the Northeast and West—regions where immigrant construction workers make up 23 % and 25 % of the labor force—by reducing available labor.

FWD.us estimates show that immigrants constitute a significant share of the U.S. construction workforce, indicating that mass deportations threaten to raise construction costs and, in turn, home prices rather than lower them.

items.subject: 💬 New thread from Citrini Analyst Team
bullets: The Trump administration imposed a 100% tariff on U.S. drones over 25 kg and a 25% tariff on smaller drones and components under Section 232, aiming to boost domestic drone production.
Allied imports receive lower rates (10‑15%) from the EU, Korea, and Japan, but the component tariffs favor UMAC’s NDAA‑compliant motors, batteries, and airframes.
Citrini’s “Drones” and “Missile Restocking” baskets are gaining traction as the tariffs shift supply chains toward U.S. manufacturers.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: The Troops Deserve Better than Hegseth
bullets: The USS Abraham Lincoln’s deployment to the Middle East in January 2026 exposed severe living‑condition complaints from sailors and families, yet Navy leadership, including CNO Adm. Daryl Caudle and Secretary Pete Hegseth, dismissed reports as “fake news” and failed to act, prompting a family town‑hall that highlighted morale, safety, and multiple overboard incidents, including a sailor who spent an hour in the water before rescue and whose wife was not informed until days later.

Hegseth’s defense of the carrier’s conditions—claiming every ship has “everything we can provide” while the Navy’s $300 billion budget could support adequate resupply—has been criticized as a cover for neglect, with calls for Hegseth, Caudle, and acting Secretary Hung Cao to visit the Lincoln and address the crew’s grievances.

items.subject: The Good Fight Tour Is Coming
bullets: The Good Fight Tour will tour Columbia, SC (Oct 16), Charlotte, NC (Oct 18), and Atlanta, GA (Oct 20) featuring Sarah, Tim, JVL, Sam, and surprise guests, with tickets selling Aug 21 and Bulwark+ members getting a presale on Aug 18.
Bulwark+ members receive early access to Bulwark LIVE events and a pre‑sale code via email on Tuesday, while Founders and Best Friends can attend a pre‑show meet‑and‑greet with the gang.

In September, Sarah and friends will hold a “How to Eat an Elephant” book tour in Washington, D.C., New York, Boston, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Chicago, and Kenyon College, with tickets already on sale.

items.subject: First Draft: Did Israel Fake the Iran Threats Against Trump’s Life?
bullets: Reuters and the Washington Post reported that U.S. officials consider recent Iranian assassination threats against Trump, which originated from Israeli intelligence, to be low‑confidence and unverified.
The alleged threat prompted Trump to secretly abandon Air Force One in Ankara, hide in a catering truck with Natalie Harp, and board an alternate plane to London, according to the Washington Post.

items.subject: The Case for a Medicare Buy-In Option
bullets: Krugman argues that while the U.S. already funds about two‑thirds of health care through government, private insurers add net negative costs via administration and fraud, making a Medicare buy‑in a pragmatic step toward universal coverage.

He notes Medicare enjoys an 82% approval rating, suggesting a public‑option framed as a Medicare expansion could overcome voter distrust of both insurers and big government, despite the political power of insurers and drug companies.

A Medicare buy‑in would let individuals and employers purchase actuarially fair Medicare coverage, reducing administrative costs and creating a “rump” private market that could later transition to full single‑payer.

items.subject: Karoline Leavitt at Her Worst: Lies and Abuse From the Podium
bullets: Karoline Leavitt, former White House Press Secretary, is accused of repeatedly spreading falsehoods and verbally attacking journalists, including claims about Gaza condoms and DEI‑caused plane crashes.
The newsletter cites specific alleged lies: her alleged friendliness with Jeffrey Epstein, the deportation of Maryland father Kilmar Abrego Garcia, and other unfounded statements.
Leavitt has announced her departure from the White House, and the piece links to a short video summarizing her most controversial remarks.

items.subject: Trump’s Gift to the Money Launderers
bullets: The Treasury announced it will destroy the government’s anti‑corruption shell‑company registry and all data collected under the Corporate Transparency Act, effectively erasing ownership records for law‑enforcement use.
Former Rep. Tom Malinowski warned the move is akin to deleting the FBI’s fingerprint database, leaving sex traffickers, drug cartels and money‑launderers free to operate unchecked.

Since Trump’s return, his administration has paused the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, exempted 99% of companies from ownership disclosure, and made the data‑destruction rule permanent, despite bipartisan support for the original law.

items.subject: Did COVID-19 Actually Come From a Lab? Two Top Scientists Debate Its Origins
bullets: Dr. Angela Rasmussen argues the virus most likely originated zoonotically, citing her own research that supports natural spillover over a lab accident.
Dr. Ashish Jha, former Biden COVID‑19 response coordinator, now backs the lab‑leak hypothesis, explaining why his view shifted after reviewing new evidence.
The segment also critiques Republican exaggeration of the lab‑leak claim and assesses U.S. pandemic preparedness, with a 46‑minute full debate available to subscribers.

items.subject: The Charlie Kirk Murder Business Gets Its Crassest Spectacle Yet
bullets: Candace Owens and Andrew Wilson are set to debate the Charlie Kirk assassination on Friday, with Owens poised to earn $300,000 if the event proceeds, despite pending smoking‑policy negotiations
The Kirk murder has sparked a MAGA civil war and unrest within Turning Point USA, fueling a lucrative “Super Bowl of Charlie murder content” that media figures are exploiting for profit

items.subject: Cheating Is All Trump Knows
bullets: Trump claimed a two‑under‑par 70 at his Bedminster club, calling it a “40 Club Championship,” but senior golfers and writer Rick Reilly say an 80‑year‑old with his swing can’t plausibly shoot ten shots under his age, implying cheating.

Conservative journalist Scott McConnell, a Trump club member, publicly called the win “cheating,” suggesting Trump’s false golf bragging reflects a broader pattern of dishonesty in his political and business claims.
The newsletter uses the golf scandal to argue that Trump’s penchant for fabricating achievements on the course mirrors his overall compulsion to cheat in politics, the economy, and deal‑making.

items.subject: The Great Burrito Discourse Isn’t Actually About Burritos
bullets: Republican influencers’ outrage over a $20 burrito split into three camps—America First blame Biden/neocons, pro‑Trump conservatives mock ‘snowflake’ complaints, and anti‑anti‑Trumpers argue the price is inflated by delivery fees—but the debate masks deeper concerns about housing affordability.

The author argues that today’s young adults face unaffordable home prices far beyond past generations, forcing them into a consumerist trap of cheap tech and food while the traditional wealth‑building path of homeownership collapses.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Trump’s Summer of Lost Causes
bullets: Trump’s White House is in crisis as Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt quits, citing maternity‑work balance, while the administration struggles to replace her unique blend of spin and dishonesty.

Trump’s domestic agenda has stalled; he is fixated on reviving weak cases like the Reflecting Pool vandalism, forcing U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro to admit the Justice Department lacks evidence and sparking a special grand jury.
The newsletter contrasts Trump’s failed pivot strategy with past bold moves, noting his current “summer of lost causes” and the broader decline of his political momentum.

items.subject: ✈️ 🚚 Moronic Trump Thinks It’s Funny He Left Toadies and the Media on Death Force One
bullets: Trump’s alleged Air Force One decoy operation, amid claims of Iranian-backed threats, was downplayed by the CIA’s low confidence and the White House’s heightened security for his family.
The newsletter criticizes Trump’s use of body doubles and “human shields,” likening him to a cartoon villain and questioning the ethics of his presidential security tactics.
Progressive defeats in Wisconsin and wins in Minnesota are framed as a call for unity to wrest Congress from the GOP, suggesting Democrats are learning from recent electoral setbacks.

items.subject: Why Isn’t the Price of Oil Even Higher?
bullets: Oil prices appear low because crude is only $25 above pre‑war levels, but the crack spread—difference between crude and refined products—has risen $35, pushing gasoline and diesel prices to $4+ and $5+ per gallon.

The widening crack spread is driven by reduced refining capacity in the Strait of Hormuz and Ukraine’s drone attacks, limiting crude processing and keeping crude prices down while refined product prices surge.

items.subject: A Minor Detail
bullets: In mid‑July, pro‑Ukrainian sources reported a drone campaign that hit dozens of commercial ships in the Sea of Azov, including vessels carrying Russian grain, prompting Russia to launch a massive retaliation that effectively sealed off Ukraine’s Black Sea ports, threatening a 50% drop in its agricultural exports.

Russia’s swift, disproportionate response coincided with a U.S.‑Turkey weapons deal delivering 70 ATACMS missiles, 12 MLRS launchers, over 2,000 cluster munitions and 47,000 howitzer rounds to Ukraine, raising fears of heightened Russia‑Turkey tensions.

The author warns that this escalation could further weaken Europe’s energy and food security ahead of a harsh winter, as Putin could leverage control of Black Sea routes and potential Turkish cooperation to pressure the EU.

items.subject: Bernie Sanders Joins Mehdi to Talk Dems, Abdul El-Sayed, AIPAC, and Netanyahu
bullets: Bernie Sanders praises recent primary wins of Democratic socialists like Abdul El‑Sayed in Michigan, criticizes Democratic leadership and the corrupt campaign‑finance system that fuels Super PACs
He says aid‑to‑Israel should be a litmus test for Democratic presidential candidates and rebuffs criticism for focusing on Netanyahu over Israel’s broader occupation
Sanders attacks John Fetterman’s Fox appearances that disparage him, while the interview is available as a 2‑minute preview for free and full video for paid subscribers

items.subject: Dem Voters Have One Weird Obsession: Winning
bullets: Democratic primary voters in Wisconsin prioritized electability, fearing a GOP governor Tom Tiffany in 2028, and chose David Crowley over Francesca Hong despite polls suggesting a 20‑point lead for Hong.

Pat Dennis of American Bridge predicted Hong’s loss, arguing that Democratic voters now judge candidates on perceived ability to win the general election, a shift distinct from Republican primary motivations.

items.subject: This Dem Uses Fox as a Platform for Hate
bullets: Michael LaRosa, former Jill Biden spokesperson, endorsed Michigan GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers on Fox’s Laura Ingraham show, accusing Democrat Abdul El‑Sayed of “cowardly” 9/11 remarks and linking him to a 2016 comment by leftist streamer Hasan Piker.

LaRosa urged El‑Sayed to publicly denounce 9/11 and even called for New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani to be barred from the 9/11 commemoration, while Rogers falsely claimed El‑Sayed believed America deserved 9/11 after his Democratic nomination.

items.subject: How to Survive a Republican Scandal: Imitate Trump
bullets: After three women accused Rep. Max Miller (R‑Ohio) of abuse, Trump called him, warned his re‑election could be in trouble, but Miller vowed to stay and praised Trump as his model for surviving scandal.

The piece cites a pattern where GOP lawmakers like Rep. Duncan Hunter, Rep. Matt Gaetz, and Rep. George Santos invoked Trump during legal crises, receiving favors such as a pardon for Santos and a failed AG nomination for Gaetz, illustrating the party’s reliance on Trump’s “felon‑in‑chief” narrative.

Rep. Cory Mills (R‑Fla.) recently blamed Democratic “lawfare” for his ethics investigation, echoing Trump’s claim that accusations are political attacks, reinforcing the newsletter’s argument that today’s GOP sees scandal survival as emulating Trump.

items.subject: Missile Restocking
bullets: The U.S. has fired more missiles and interceptors in the first five months of 2026 than in any year since Desert Storm, driven by Russian and Iranian advances in autonomous drones and ballistic missiles, and the FY2027 DoW budget proposes a nearly 5‑fold increase in missile spending.

Patriot and THAAD stockpiles have been depleted by ~66% and ~44% respectively, with CSIS noting no viable alternatives, exposing a critical vulnerability in U.S. and allied missile defense that the administration is addressing through expanded production capacity and increased competition among prime contractors.

The defense industrial base faces systemic constraints—limited production capacity, fragile supply chains, and long lead times—leading to a shift from a 20‑year consolidation of prime contractors to a new strategy of capacity expansion and anti‑competitive oligopoly mitigation to meet urgent demand signals.

items.subject: It’s Black Voters, Stupid. And Thank God for That.
bullets: The author argues Democratic primary success now hinges on African‑American voters, noting they remain the party’s backbone while DSA‑aligned candidates like Abdul El‑Sayed underperform with Black voters despite strong poll numbers.
Wisconsin polls lagged behind rapid voter shifts, missing David Crowley’s surge from 22% to 39.8% after Mandela Barnes dropped out, illustrating real‑time polling latency rather than inaccuracy.
Mike Lindell’s Trump‑endorsed bid for Minnesota governor collapsed, failing to break 50% even in the state’s most pro‑Trump counties, underscoring the limits of MAGA brand appeal.

William Kristol predicts a Democratic blue wave in November

items.subject: The Writer and the Sea
bullets: The essay uses Genesis’s primordial water and firmament myth to argue that ancient creation stories are symbolic narratives about separating chaos into ordered worlds, not scientific accounts.

It links writers’ fascination with the sea—citing Hemingway’s Cuban voyages and Borges’s comparison of the ocean to Dostoevsky—to illustrate how the sea serves as a metaphor for discovery and new worlds for storytellers.
