items.subject: MAGA Has Found Its New Favorite Culture War
bullets: Bill Cassidy’s emotional floor speech failed to sway the Senate vote that confirmed Todd Blanche as Attorney General, highlighting the GOP’s internal divisions on judicial appointments.

Tucker Carlson’s recent interviews with Hunter Biden and his monologue echoing presidential rhetoric suggest a pivot toward a campaign‑style media strategy, raising questions about his influence on the 2024 race.

The DSA‑aligned Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong’s candidacy is portrayed as a high‑stakes experiment in a swing state, underscoring the Democrats’ willingness to test progressive platforms in key battlegrounds.

items.subject: Trump Is Now Openly Flirting With Attacking the Midterms
bullets: Trump told far‑right host Wayne Allyn Root that declaring a national emergency over the midterms could be a viable alternative to the stalled SAVE Act, hinting at a potential coup against U.S. democracy.

Francesca Hong, the democratic socialist once seen as the Democratic nominee for Wisconsin governor, lost a tight primary to moderate David Crowley, while Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan won the Senate primary, boosting the left’s prospects.

Exclusive polling shows the Kansas Senate race is nearly tied, a rare scenario as the state has not elected a Democrat to the upper chamber in 96 years, underscoring the high electoral stakes nationwide.

items.subject: Why you can’t find a primary care doctor
bullets: Over 100 million Americans lack primary care, driven by a fee‑for‑service system that pays $259 per visit versus $1,092 for a gastroenterology visit, leading to an 87,000‑doctor shortfall by 2037.

Primary care doctors face 15‑minute visits, 45 % burnout, and 39 % plan to stop seeing patients, deepening shortages; solutions include value‑based payment, expanded residency slots, and AI‑driven admin reduction.

Patients can mitigate the gap by seeking community health centers, skilled NPs/​PAs, telehealth, and becoming proactive advocates—preparing concise concerns, a one‑page health summary, and asking targeted questions.

items.subject: The Rise of the Measles-Industrial Complex
bullets: Trump’s executive order threatens to cut U.S. child vaccination rates, coinciding with a measles surge that has already surpassed last year’s worst season since 1991; scientific studies find no vaccine‑autism link, but air‑pollution exposure does correlate with higher autism rates.

Vaccination skepticism is now a predominantly Republican stance, with Gallup polls showing a decade‑long decline in belief in vaccine importance and a rise in perceived danger, though it remains a minority view within the party.

Anti‑vax sentiment is tied to a lucrative right‑wing “snake‑oil” industry and a broader anti‑intellectual culture war, amplified by figures like Dr. Mehmet Oz and COVID‑era conspiracy narratives, ensuring the political momentum persists beyond Trump’s tenure.

items.subject: Vaccine Lies, Direct from the Oval Office
bullets: Donald Trump signed an executive order to cut the U.S. childhood vaccine schedule from 17 to 11 shots and split the combined MMR vaccine into three separate injections, despite likely legal challenges similar to a blocked HHS rule by Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

The order could pressure states to relax school vaccine mandates and, combined with presidential rhetoric, may boost parental vaccine hesitancy as measles cases rise to 2,465 this year—already surpassing last year’s record high since 1991—and pertussis cases also climb.

Kennedy, a longtime anti‑vaccine activist, has driven the schedule change push from HHS, and Trump has publicly supported his efforts, even expressing frustration that Kennedy isn’t moving faster on the agenda.

items.subject: Amanda Carpenter: Audit the White House
bullets: Amanda Carpenter argues that Trump’s pardon power can’t shield those profiting from shady contracts, citing forfeiture and seizure laws that could strip them of money and restore taxpayer funds.
She links China’s $100 million donation to Trump’s cryptocurrency firm to his soft‑on‑China stance, suggesting a bribery motive behind his policies.
Carpenter notes Trump’s use of a catering cart to exit Turkey, claims the White House is engaging in socialist‑style company takeovers, and warns the National Guard will remain in DC until 2029.

items.subject: 'I've Been Handed a Death Sentence, and My Crime Is Being a Cancer Patient From Gaza'
bullets: Um Mahmoud, a Gaza-born cancer patient diagnosed in 2020, was receiving treatment in Ramallah when Israel’s 2023 war on Gaza began, leaving her trapped in the West Bank without care.
The Palestinian Authority can no longer fund her treatment because Israel has withheld tax revenues, forcing Um Mahmoud to wait while her cancer worsens.
Her case illustrates how Israel’s genocide in Gaza extends beyond the conflict zone, crippling healthcare access for Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

items.subject: Trump’s America Is Really Hulk Hogan’s America
bullets: The newsletter argues that professional wrestling, especially Vince McMahon’s story in Josie Riesman’s Ringmaster, serves as a Rosetta Stone for understanding Trumpism and MAGA.
It promotes a new book linking Hulk Hogan’s career and persona to Donald Trump’s authoritarian style, claiming the comparison will fundamentally reshape readers’ view of Trump.
The piece is offered as a free teaser for Bulwark+, urging readers to try the subscription to access the full analysis.

Pro-Israel super PACs may raise and spend $250 million this election cycle

bullets: Democrats plan a “death by a thousand cuts” strategy of subpoenas, hearings, and criminal referrals to slow Trump’s administration if they win the 2026 House majority, targeting corruption, ICE killings, and Iran war missteps.

Trump’s White House is preparing for a Democratic takeover with defiance of Congress, while Trump signs an executive order on vaccines and Bill Cassidy publicly rejects anti‑vaccine conspiracy theories.

items.subject: The U.S. Healthcare System is Already Mostly Socialized
bullets: Krugman argues that U.S. healthcare is already largely socialized, noting that government programs (Medicare, Medicaid, ACA subsidies, and tax‑free employer premiums) cover over two‑thirds of insurance spending, amounting to roughly $400 billion in subsidies annually.

He cites Medicare’s 82% favorable rating and Medicaid’s 73% rating versus widespread dislike of private insurers, and points out that private plans like Medicare Advantage overpaid by $84 billion due to upcoding, suggesting insurers act as costly parasites.

Consequently, Krugman frames Abdul El‑Sayed’s Medicare‑for‑All proposal not as radical socialism but as a logical step to eliminate the inefficient, partially privatized system and fund care progressively through taxes.

items.subject: EO for routine childhood vaccines, Covid-19, fire, heat, and more
bullets: The FDA enforcement report revealed 236,192 lettuce cases recalled, mostly from Walmart, not Taco Bell, and Michigan’s cyclosporiasis outbreak is nearly over with zero new infections, so leafy greens are safe again.

A Salmonella outbreak linked to Sinaloa jalapeños has sickened 345 people in 27 states, 36 hospitalized, with 2 antibiotic‑resistant cases; avoid jalapeños and foods from retailers like Walmart, Target, and Whole Foods until the recall clears.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: Can Francesca Hong Win? Yes. Is She the Most Electable? Probably Not.
bullets: Francesca Hong can win Wisconsin’s governor race because the state is a 50‑50 swing and the Republican opponent, Tom Tiffany, is a weak MAGA candidate, but her DSA label and leftward stance make her less electable than establishment favorite David Crowley, who aligns with Governor Evers and avoids controversial socialist branding

A July Marquette poll showed Hong trailing Tiffany by 3 points among registered voters and tied among likely voters, while Crowley wasn’t tested; independent voters (52%) view the DSA unfavorably, and about half of national voters say they’re less likely to support a democratic socialist candidate

Pfeiffer argues that while electability is uncertain, data‑center policy (76% of voters favor a moratorium) and Hong’s bold change message contrast with Crowley’s continuity‑plus approach, leading him to conclude Crowley has the better chance of winning in November

items.subject: James Fishback Wanted a Scandal. He Got One.
bullets: James Fishback’s attempt to revive his Florida governor campaign by accusing Rep. Byron Donalds of a DOJ probe backfired, as the DOJ publicly cleared Donalds and warned against false accusations.
Fishback now faces a $11,000 scholarship lawsuit from former debater Briana Whatley, plus a $1.5 million debt to former employer Greenlight Capital, which has seized his assets.
Former staffer Gianna Tagliarini reported Fishback to state law enforcement over his anti‑woke debate operation, potentially prompting a new investigation.

items.subject: Why Ben Shapiro Is Wrong About Me, Islamophobia, and His Dumb New Movie
bullets: Mehdi argues Ben Shapiro’s 13‑minute video defending the Daily Wire’s new film is itself Islamophobic, claiming the movie perpetuates negative Muslim stereotypes and miscounts Muslim villains in Hollywood.
He contends the Daily Wire’s focus on ISIS‑themed films is a deliberate distraction from Israel’s actions in Gaza, labeling it a propaganda tactic.
Mehdi offers a 7‑minute rebuttal video with “receipts” to support his critique and invites viewers to subscribe for uncensored content.

items.subject: Why Do People Linked to Jeffrey Epstein Keep Mysteriously Dying?
bullets: In the past decade, nine people linked to Epstein—including former partners, employees and alleged associates—have died from causes ranging from cancer and overdose to suicide, often under mysterious circumstances

items.subject: “The People” Are Lying Liars
bullets: A focus group with three-time Trump‑voting Republicans in South Carolina discussed Lindsey Graham, Donald Trump and other topics, providing data that supports the author’s claim that “everybody lies.”
The author argues that people are inherently messy, contradictory, and do not reason deductively, suggesting a deeper, darker view of human behavior than the usual “people lie” shorthand.

items.subject: Will Tucker Carlson Run For President? Sam Seder Thinks ‘It’s Bullsh*t’
bullets: Sam Seder argues the Democratic establishment is out of touch, likening its insurgency to a Tea Party‑style movement and highlighting progressive wins across the country.
Seder and Mehdi dissect the 2025 Jubilee debate, claiming it exposed the core motivations of young MAGA conservatives and the stakes of their movement.

They preview the upcoming “Great Tucker Carlson Debate,” questioning whether Carlson should run for president, his trustworthiness on Israel and foreign wars, and the value of appearing on his platform.

bullets: Hunter Biden revealed Joe Biden’s metastatic prostate cancer has spread to his bones, causing severe pain yet he remains active, prompting condolences from the author.

Ohio Rep. Max Miller faces abuse allegations; GOP leaders Trump and Speaker Johnson back him, while most House Republicans refuse to discuss or oppose his re‑election despite calls from Sen. Bernie Moreno.

Sen. Bill Cassidy and Sen. John Cornyn voted to confirm Todd Blanche as Attorney General, ignoring Epstein survivors’ concerns, citing DOJ progress on human trafficking as justification, highlighting GOP tolerance of sexual‑assault cover‑ups.

items.subject: At Last, a Real Fighter to Punch Back at Trump
bullets: Abdul El‑Sayed’s Senate campaign in Michigan opened with aggressive, Trump‑style counter‑punches to hostile anchors, positioning him as a rare Democratic “fighter” in the Trump era.
El‑Sayed sharply rebuked Trump’s Islamophobic post comparing their wives, delivering a brutal response that Republicans fear could become a new Democratic counter‑punch model.

items.subject: What Malta Tells Us About Oligarchy
bullets: Malta, with 500,000 residents, hosts over $500 billion in foreign direct investment and an equal amount of outbound investment, largely through shell companies that shift profits to its near‑zero corporate tax rate, costing the U.S. an estimated $100 billion annually in lost tax revenue.

Krugman argues this profit‑shifting exemplifies a broader oligarchic trend: tax avoidance/evasion enriches the wealthy, reinforcing their political power, while the EU’s weak enforcement and the U.S. under Trump have stalled global minimum‑15% corporate tax efforts.
He warns that without a major political shift, the cumulative effect of such tax shelters will continue to erode public programs, calling Malta a vivid illustration of the systemic problem.

items.subject: What Happens When an Election Denier Runs a Crucial Swing State?
bullets: Democratic leaders warn that GOP nominee Tom Tiffany, a former House Republican who voted to overturn the 2020 results and backs election‑lie lawsuits, could jeopardize certification of Wisconsin’s 2028 presidential and Senate elections if elected governor.

The race also determines control of Wisconsin’s redistricting; a Democratic win would let the party redraw maps for 2028, potentially adding safe Democratic House seats, while a Republican trifecta could erase them.

Parallel gubernatorial contests in Arizona and Pennsylvania feature other election‑denying Republicans, but Wisconsin’s open governor’s seat makes the stakes uniquely acute for national election integrity.

items.subject: 8 Unanswered Questions About Jeffrey Epstein’s Death
bullets: Congress passed a law forcing the Justice Department to release Epstein’s files, but the Trump administration allegedly stalled and blocked meetings with victims.
The article lists eight unresolved issues, starting with why required inmate checks were skipped, highlighting procedural failures that fuel suicide doubts.

items.subject: Why Losing Battles are Worth Fighting
bullets: The preview of the latest Triad Mailbag episode features JVL answering listener questions on DSA candidates, census protection, Ross Douthat on “60 Minutes,” Republican authoritarianism, Tolkien’s “long defeat,” Ezra Klein, site redesign, fan shout‑outs, World Cup jerseys, future books, music, comics, and cultural pet‑peeves.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: How Trump's Grip on the GOP Is Slipping — One Primary at a Time
bullets: Trump's 2023 vengeance campaign knocked out several GOP incumbents, but recent primary defeats of his endorsed candidates—like in Indiana and against Thomas Massie—show his influence is waning.

In 2022 Trump’s kingmaker push backfired, elevating weak candidates such as Herschel Walker and Dr. Oz who lost, prompting him to defer to party professionals and even withdraw support for less electable MAGA hopefuls.

The notable exception was his backing of Ken Paxton in the Texas GOP runoff, defying operatives who deemed John Cornyn more viable, highlighting Trump’s selective and increasingly contested endorsements.

items.subject: ‘Republicans Are Trying To Distract You’: Former Wisconsin Democratic Leader Lays Out How to Win in November
bullets: Former Wisconsin Democratic Party chair Ben Wikler outlines a strategy to counter GOP gerrymandering, power grabs and voter suppression, detailed in his new book “This Is the Plan.”
Wikler warns that Republican gubernatorial candidate Tom Tiffany is part of a broader effort to distract voters from economic hardships while Democratic socialist Francesca Hong runs against him.
The Substack Live featured a Q&A where Wikler discussed his plan to reclaim Wisconsin democracy and urged Democrats to mobilize for the November elections.

items.subject: How to Break the Fifty-Year Stalemate on Childcare Policy
bullets: In 1971 Nixon vetoed a bipartisan childcare bill after adviser Pat Buchanan warned it would be “family‑weakening,” starting a half‑century stalemate over federal childcare policy.

Project 2029, a Democratic‑aligned think tank, proposes a massive childcare package that lets families choose between federally funded universal care or direct cash assistance, aiming to win Republican support.
Elliot Haspel says the plan reflects an evolution in Democratic thinking, recognizing diverse family needs and offering a simple, choice‑based system to finally break the longstanding impasse.

items.subject: Against Oligarchy, Part III: Taxing Capital vs. Taxing Labor
bullets: Since 2000 the labor share of U.S. income has fallen sharply while the capital share has surged, a trend Krugman links to rising AI investment that favors capital over workers.
He argues that tax policy shifts since the 1970s have increasingly favored capital—lower rates on dividends, capital gains, and corporate profits—amplifying both income and wealth inequality.
Krugman calls for reversing the pro‑capital tax bias, warning that without it the AI‑driven economy will further concentrate wealth in the hands of a billionaire oligarchy.

items.subject: Endangered Specious
bullets: Energy Secretary Chris Wright, appointed by Trump, has overseen a rapid revival of Venezuela’s oil output, pushing exports above 1 million barrels per day for three consecutive months after a December low of half that level.

In response to the Iran‑war‑induced oil shock, Wright launched a scaled‑up SPR oil‑exchange program that loans barrels to companies with a premium of up to 24%, returning 35‑40 million barrels of extra oil by next year without congressional approval or taxpayer cost.

items.subject: Meet the Former Trump White House Lawyer Who Says Our Democracy Could Be ‘Screwed’ in 2026
bullets: Former Trump White House lawyer Ty Cobb warns that American democracy could be effectively “screwed” by 2026, doubting its survival under Trump’s influence.
Cobb bluntly claims the new Attorney General Todd Blanche may try to discredit midterm results and suggests Trump’s corruption exceeds even Vladimir Putin’s.
The interview, recorded before Blanche’s Senate confirmation, includes Cobb’s answers about the Mueller report’s ten alleged obstruction episodes and his regrets working for Trump.

items.subject: Trump Gave Democrats an Opening on Immigration. They’re Afraid to Take It.
bullets: Democrats publicly condemn Trump’s deportation violence but have omitted ICE reform from their midterm agenda, despite internal briefings highlighting a $270 billion ICE budget lasting to 2033 and low ICE approval ratings.
Immigration advocacy groups urged House Democrats to seize the issue with stories, hearings, and field visits, noting a Fox poll shows voters now trust Democrats on immigration more than Republicans.
Nevertheless, many Democratic campaigns consider anti‑ICE messaging too risky so close to the November election, leaving the party largely paralyzed on the issue.

items.subject: This Week in Palestine: UNICEF Reports 300 Palestinian Children Killed in 300 Days, as Israel Destroys Gaza Medici…
bullets: UNICEF reports 300 Palestinian children killed in 300 days, averaging one child per day, since the October ceasefire claim, highlighting ongoing Israeli violence in Gaza.
Israel destroyed medical supply warehouses in Gaza on August 1, further crippling healthcare access amid continued attacks on civilians and settlements.
The newsletter notes over 30 Palestinians killed in the days after U.S. President Trump announced a breakthrough in ceasefire talks, underscoring the lack of a genuine truce.

Mitchell Jackson recounts his time at Vice magazine

items.subject: South Carolina’s Surprise Election (with Meg Kinnard)
bullets: South Carolina’s special Republican primary to replace late Sen. Lindsey Graham features his sister, Sen. Darline Graham, backed by President Trump, but polls and focus groups show she faces strong intra‑party challengers.
The episode examines Lindsey Graham’s legacy among South Carolina Republicans and the rapid, unexpected nature of the special election, with insights from AP reporter Meg Kinnard.

items.subject: Why the Michigan Polls Blew It — And What It Means for November
bullets: Michigan polls were wildly inaccurate, turning an expected El‑Sayed victory into a close race that wasn’t called until the next morning, highlighting severe polling errors in the state.
The author questions whether this polling failure is limited to the Democratic primary or will persist into the general election, suggesting a risk of continued polling panic before November.
He also asks why no exit polls were conducted in Michigan, speculating on legal or funding issues, and notes the absence of this critical data as a significant concern.

items.subject: As Goes Ohio...
bullets: The author contrasts Ohio GOP hopeful Vivek Ramaswamy’s “conservativemaxxing” platform with former health official Amy Acton’s nostalgic appeal to Ohio’s past politics.

Ramaswamy promises tax‑cut schemes like free electricity for data centers, while voters, recalling Missouri’s defeat of an income‑tax repeal, remain skeptical about eliminating state and property taxes.
With 88 days to the election, the author will continue on‑the‑ground reporting from Ohio’s Buckeye state and invites readers to discuss which aspects of “politics of yesteryear” might be revived.

items.subject: Feigning Surprise
bullets: US sanctions have failed to halt China’s rapid progress in semiconductors and AI, with firms like DeepSeek and Moonshot releasing competitive models and China mass‑producing deep‑ultraviolet chip tools and an extreme‑ultraviolet prototype, a capability long deemed Western‑only.

Doomberg has repeatedly warned that sanctions actually accelerate China’s chip dominance, publishing forecasts in April 2024, May 2025, May 2024 and July 2024 that predicted the very breakthroughs now reported by The Information.

items.subject: Talking With G. Elliott Morris About the Midterms
bullets: G. Elliott Morris’s Strength in Numbers model gives Democrats an 87% chance to win the House, estimating they’ll secure about 231 seats, though gerrymandering likely costs them 5‑6 seats versus a 95‑96% chance without it

The Senate forecast shows Democrats at a 54% chance to capture control, needing four pickups; they’re favored in North Carolina (≈85% chance) and see toss‑up prospects in Maine, Texas, Alaska and Ohio, while defending a vulnerable Michigan seat

Morris argues polling shows Abdul El‑Sayed’s odds in Michigan are statistically indistinguishable from a more moderate Democrat, contradicting pundit claims that his progressive stance makes a Democratic Senate win unlikely

items.subject: We May Need ‘Massive Boycotts’ to Stop Trump, Says Democracy Expert
bullets: Democracy Forward’s Skye Perryman warned that massive boycotts and work stoppages may become necessary to counter the Trump‑Vance administration’s alleged election‑rigging ahead of the 2026 midterms.
Zeteo’s four‑part ‘Start the Steal’ series details how the Trump‑Vance team is using authoritarian tactics to rig elections and how nonprofits, activists, and Democrats are fighting back.
A recent town hall with Zeteo host Mehdi, Asawin “Swin” Suebsaeng, and Perryman discussed voter threats, potential coups, and the impact of collective action forcing the administration to back down.

items.subject: This Week in Democracy – Week 81: Trump’s Corruption Is Off the Charts
bullets: Abdul El‑Sayed won the Michigan Senate primary against a $60 million AIPAC‑backed field, showing voters can defeat well‑funded opponents; Trump’s Justice Department is pushing to dismiss Jan. 6 charges against Oath Keepers while ICE collected DNA from ~920,000 immigrants in 2025, many never convicted.

Trump launched a $100,000‑per‑month premium Truth Social API that could let traders profit from his posts; he also signed executive orders to restrict birthright citizenship and to limit foreign births, despite a Supreme Court ruling upholding the right.

ICE’s 2025 DNA collection became the largest new source for the FBI’s criminal database, and the Trump administration is again attempting to remove Fed Governor Lisa Cook after a Supreme Court decision allowed her to stay in office.

items.subject: The GOAT Episode
bullets: JVL and Tim hosted a large show featuring Callista Gingrich’s uncanny performance, Thom Tillis’s new “burn book,” Tucker Carlson’s presidential run, and a discussion on burrito discourse, all highlighted as a classic episode.

items.subject: The Government Shouldn’t Pick Winners and Losers in Media
bullets: The FCC voted to eliminate the 39% national ownership cap, allowing media giants like Sinclair to consolidate local stations, a move defended by FCC Chair Brendan Carr as a case‑by‑case review of localism, viewpoint diversity, and competition.

Free Press argues the FCC lacks authority to lift the cap without congressional action, warning that the change will enable a few dominant broadcasters to dominate markets, cut journalist jobs, and flood local news with low‑quality content.

items.subject: Pakistanis 'Massively Disappointed' in Trump and the U.S., Says Top Imran Khan Adviser
bullets: Zulfi Bukhari, top adviser to imprisoned ex‑PM Imran Khan, says Khan has been in solitary confinement for seven months with no medical bail granted.
Bukhari criticises former President Trump, saying Pakistanis feel "massively disappointed" that the U.S. has not advocated for Khan despite promises.
He denies any current negotiations to free Khan, contradicting an Observer report about a behind‑the‑scenes deal.

items.subject: News of the Weak (Labor Market)
bullets: The latest jobs report showed a loss of 23,000 jobs versus a forecast of 80,000 gains, and revisions to earlier months reveal much weaker overall employment growth during Trump’s term than previously thought.

Krugman argues that anti‑immigration policies have cut the labor‑force pool, so low job creation (about 26,000 per month) no longer translates into higher unemployment, but also fails to free jobs for native‑born workers, as immigrant losses are matched by a drop in total employment.

Wage growth is slowing and the Conference Board’s labor‑market differential has fallen sharply, indicating weaker bargaining power and a less optimistic perception of job availability despite Trump’s claims of a booming economy.

items.subject: Blanche on the Bubble
bullets: Putin may test NATO with a limited assault on a member country, per U.S. intelligence cited by the WSJ, amid U.S. munitions stockpiles falling dangerously low.

July’s job loss hit 23,000, with May and June revised down 103,000, while the unemployment rate fell to 4.1% as 260,000 people exited the labor force, leaving 30% of the unemployed job‑hungry for over six months.

Sen. Bill Cassidy, after voting to convict Trump and confirming RFK Jr., faces pressure from Murkowski and could oppose Todd Blanche’s DOJ nomination, reflecting his uneasy stance toward Trump‑aligned Republicans like Thom Tillis.

items.subject: 🚨TODAY, 2pm ET, Live Q&A: 'Start the Steal,' Discussion with Mehdi and Swin
bullets: Donald Trump and allies are actively attempting to rig the 2024 midterm elections, as detailed in Zeteo’s four-part ‘Start the Steal’ series, citing legal challenges and voter suppression tactics.
Democratic officials and nonprofits, including Democracy Forward’s president Skye Perryman, are countering these efforts through court battles and public advocacy.
A live Q&A with Mehdi, Swin (co-author of the series), and Perryman will air Friday at 2pm ET to discuss the series and answer audience questions.

items.subject: Protection Matters
bullets: Agentic AI coding agents have sparked a surge in cyberattacks, prompting a sharp rally in cybersecurity stocks that outperformed AI infrastructure and semiconductor sectors since Q1 2024.

The newsletter argues AI will fuel a near‑term cybersecurity boom, but only firms with hard enforcement points—hardware, telemetry, data or distribution—will retain durable market share, while vulnerability‑management vendors face commoditization risk.

Recent incidents, like OpenAI’s rogue agent breaching Hugging Face and Iranian attacks on US water systems, illustrate the escalating threat landscape and the growing budgets shifting toward AI‑driven security solutions.

items.subject: Here Come the Super-Islamophobic Midterms
bullets: Abdul El‑Sayed, a Muslim former Detroit health official, secured the Democratic Senate nomination in Michigan, prompting a wave of Republican outrage that the author frames as a new wave of overt Islamophobia.
The piece cites Muslim‑American scholar Dalia Mogahed, noting that spikes in Islamophobia historically align more with political events than terrorist attacks, challenging common narratives.

It also warns of escalating tensions: Israeli troops allegedly assaulted Palestinian‑American citizens, and Donald Trump is furious over a Washington Post story claiming he’s at odds with Pete Hegseth over the Iran war fallout.

items.subject: Senate Voting to Give Trump a Tariff Nuke
bullets: A bipartisan bill, the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act, is moving through Congress with 62 Senate cosponsors (including 21 Democrats) and could clear the Senate soon.
If passed, the bill would let the president impose 100% tariffs on any country indefinitely, granting near‑absolute tariff authority that even the Supreme Court couldn’t overturn.

items.subject: Lying Liars Lie to Each Other Too
bullets: Trump has publicly berated his own officials—AG Jeannine Pirro, RFK Jr., and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth—over contractor failures, vaccine misinformation claims, and false munitions reports, highlighting internal lies.

Legal scholars note the collapse of the ‘presumption of regularity’: courts now demand evidence of government truthfulness in grand‑jury cases, dismissing charges seen as vindictive prosecutions under Trump II.

The administration’s bad‑faith policies—re‑imposing tariffs on 60 nations, cutting food‑stamp benefits, and denying FEMA aid to blue states—combined with Pentagon misinformation have depleted precision munitions in the Iran war, creating self‑inflicted national‑security disasters.

items.subject: How Trump Is Turning the U.S. Intel Community Into an Election-Rigging Machine
bullets: Ian Bassin, former Obama White House lawyer, says Trump is turning U.S. intelligence agencies into tools for personal power, a tactic he likens to dictators’ playbooks.

Trump‑backed Georgia election officials have been in contact with a White House election‑security official, showing coordination between the administration and the election‑denial movement at the local level.

Two senior U.S. officials told Zeteo that no classified evidence exists of foreign interference in the 2020 election, yet aides repeatedly fed Trump false assurances to sustain his false claim of a stolen election.

He convened with former allies like Marjorie Taylor Greene, Thomas Massie, and Joe Kent, who now criticize Trump and promote a non‑Trump 2028 option, while critics argue Carlson is a Putin‑influenced dupe with radical party ambitions

items.subject: Our Chaos Agent President Has Another Big Card to Play
bullets: Michigan GOP primary shock: Trump‑endorsed Amir Hassan lost 33% to Tom Smith, who had dropped out months earlier, winning 50% in a surprise upset that highlighted Trump’s endorsement power limits.

Trump’s 2024 election strategy hinges on a contested executive order to restrict mail‑in voting; the Supreme Court may lift a stay, giving the administration broad discretion to alter ballot delivery before November, risking chaotic midterm elections.

A Russian‑backed strike on a Moscow restaurant during a birthday for Aerospace Forces commander Alexander Chaiko killed five, injured nineteen, and may implicate Ukraine, which has targeted Chaiko for his role in the 2022 Kyiv offensive and Bucha occupation.

items.subject: Even Wolf Blitzer Is Baffled by John Fetterman's Pro-Israel Obsession
bullets: Senator John Fetterman told CNN’s Wolf Blitzer he would consider leaving the Democratic Party if its platform adopted anti‑Israel positions, framing Israel support as a personal “red line.”

Blitzer highlighted AIPAC’s $30 million spend backing Rep. Haley Stevens and potential multi‑million support for GOP Mike Rogers, questioning why Fetterman makes a foreign issue his defining litmus test.
New Maine polls show progressive Troy Jackson overtaking GOP Sen. Susan Collins, while Donald Trump’s fluctuating stance on Iran continues to dominate headlines.

items.subject: The Good News Trump Won’t Mention
bullets: U.S. murder rates, which spiked after Covid, have been falling and are now near 1960s lows in major cities like New York, a trend credited by many to Biden‑era social programs such as the American Rescue Plan.

Krugman argues Trump stays silent on declining crime because he despises cities, clings to an outdated 1980s view of urban violence, and uses punitive rhetoric as a political end, not a means to improve safety.
He notes Trump’s false claims routinely ignore positive developments, preferring to blame “radical left” pollsters while promoting a narrative of cruelty and punishment.

items.subject: Trump Wants To Steal the Midterms – But the Dems Actually Have A Plan To Fight Back
bullets: Democratic officials nationwide are conducting “wargames” to prepare for scenarios where Trump could deploy armed federal agents or troops to polling places, treating the president as a primary election threat.

The administration’s alleged tactics include voter intimidation, illegal ballot‑seizing attempts, and threats to use the Insurrection Act, prompting a massive, coordinated defensive effort by Democrats, legal nonprofits, and election officials.
Sources say the preparation mirrors defenses against foreign adversaries, emphasizing the need for overwhelming voter turnout to counter Trump’s authoritarian strategy.

items.subject: Capital One Just Dropped an Atomic Bomb on Trump (w/ Andrew Weissmann)
bullets: Sam Stein and Andrew Weissmann say the Justice Department’s dismissal of Lincoln Memorial reflecting‑pool damage charges leaves Olympian David Hearn with limited recourse and prompts a sharp Trump response.

They flag Todd Blanche’s uncertain Senate confirmation, a proposed “anti‑weaponization” fund with tax‑immunity provisions, and Capital One’s claim that Trump Organization accounts violated anti‑money‑laundering rules.
They note Anthony Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment before Congress, and promote Weissmann’s new book Liar’s Kingdom and the Illegal News podcast.

items.subject: Why Bari Weiss's Boss Is Full of ‘Horseshit’
bullets: Paramount CEO David Ellison’s New York Times op‑ed defending his politics and suitability to run CNN is being dismissed by CBS and CNN insiders as a desperate PR stunt to salvage the faltering $111 billion WarnerMount merger.

Sources say the piece reads like lawyer‑crafted copy, likely orchestrated by investment banker Blair Effron, and portrays Ellison as a misunderstood victim despite evidence he’s a right‑wing partisan.

items.subject: The Brutal Path Ahead for El-Sayed
bullets: Abdul El‑Sayed delivered a tentative victory speech after a razor‑thin primary win over Rep. Haley Stevens, urging unity to block GOP nominee Mike Rogers and Donald Trump in the Senate race.
He highlighted his immigrant background, pledged to unite Democratic voters, and warned he has only 91 days to win over skeptical constituents before the general election.

items.subject: The Case Against El-Sayed Doomerism
bullets: El‑Sayed won the Michigan Democratic Senate primary but his lead has collapsed from +13 in polls to about +1% after an 11‑to‑1 spending disadvantage, raising concerns about his appeal to Black voters in Wayne and Oakland counties and his margin in Macomb.

Despite Michigan’s long Democratic Senate streak and a favorable environment, Republican Mike Rogers—who earned 48.3% in 2024 and has a solid 2.7 million‑voter base—could force a tight race decided by fewer than 50,000 votes.

A recent civilian medevac crash in New Mexico, caused by GPS jamming from a military exercise, marks the first U.S. plane loss linked to drone‑warfare‑related interference, highlighting emerging aviation risks.

items.subject: The Supreme Court Shredded America’s ‘Most Powerful’ Law
bullets: The Supreme Court this year gutted key provisions of the Voting Rights Act, putting over a dozen Black‑led House districts at risk of elimination.
Republicans are pushing the SAVE America Act, which would further restrict voting access for Black and brown voters, intensifying concerns about voter suppression.

items.subject: It’s Still a Blue Wave
bullets: Republican senators must abstain from voting on Todd Blanche’s attorney‑general nomination; Susan Collins already opposes him and only one other senator—likely Murkowski, Cassidy, or another—can also abstain without endangering the nomination

Michigan Democratic Senate primary appears tighter than polls predicted, with left‑wing Abdul El‑Sayed likely winning by only 1‑2 points, improving Republican Mike Rogers’ chances in the general but not guaranteeing a pickup

Democrats have a slightly better than 50‑50 chance of retaining Senate control, aided by Max Miller’s scandal in Ohio, potential pickups in North Carolina, Maine, Alaska, Iowa, Texas, and vulnerable GOP incumbents in Kansas, South Dakota, Idaho, and possibly Montana

items.subject: Here's Exactly How Abdul El-Sayed Beats Mike Rogers
bullets: Abdul El‑Sayed won Michigan’s Senate primary against Mike Rogers, surviving an 11‑to‑1 spending disadvantage from Super PACs tied to AIPAC, the DSCC, and other special interests, with $60 million spent against him.

El‑Sayed’s victory challenges traditional political rules, signaling a backlash against an establishment that relies on heavy outside spending and an outdated view of politics, though critics argue he lacks the strength of former Senator Stevens and may need to broaden his appeal for November.

items.subject: Will This Be AIPAC’s Biggest Defeat – Ever?
bullets: AIPAC spent $30 million and other pro‑Israel donors added $30 million to help Congresswoman Haley Stevens win Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, but Abdul El‑Sayed ultimately prevailed, with NBC calling the race for him before 2 am ET.
El‑Sayed’s victory was framed as a David‑vs‑Goliath win against AIPAC and the establishment, with former candidate Mallory McMorrow endorsing him after dropping out.
The campaign’s close finish and the heavy spending highlight a significant setback for AIPAC, marking what the newsletter calls its most expensive and costly defeat yet.

items.subject: The system should be on trial too.
bullets: 70% of U.S. women say they wanted more info on postpartum mental health before birth, yet only 6% of UK pregnant women receive any antenatal education on postpartum psychosis, a condition affecting as many families as Down syndrome annually.

Postpartum care lacks a clear owner: Lindsay Clancy accessed multiple providers and 13 psychiatric meds within weeks of her children’s deaths, but fragmented records prevented any clinician from seeing the full picture.

In FY2023 NIH allocated just $4.6 billion to women’s health—about one‑tenth of its $45 billion budget—leaving postpartum psychosis without a formal diagnosis, screening tool, or adequate research funding.

items.subject: An Explosion of Misery
bullets: Trump’s administration imposed work‑verification requirements on SNAP, causing millions—especially children—to lose $187‑a‑month food aid, despite most recipients already working irregularly.

Republican refusal to extend the Biden‑era ACA subsidy fix eliminated the subsidy cliff, leaving middle‑income families (just above 400% of poverty) without aid and dropping enrollment by about three million, increasing under‑insurance.

Krugman argues these cuts create an "explosion of misery" that not only deepens poverty now but reduces long‑term economic growth, as evidence shows nutrition and health assistance yields high societal returns.

items.subject: LIVE From Michigan: Mehdi and Prem on Abdul El-Sayed
bullets: The Michigan Senate Democratic primary pits progressive Abdul El‑Sayed against AIPAC‑backed centrist Haley Stevens, who holds a roughly nine‑to‑one fundraising advantage.

Zeteo’s live two‑hour stream featured progressive figures like Rep. Ilhan Omar, newcomers Chris Rabb and Brad Lander, plus experts discussing AIPAC’s influence, Islamophobia, and the race’s stakes for establishment Democrats.
View the full coverage video to catch all interviews and analysis as Michigan continues tallying votes into the night.

items.subject: Here Are 19 - Yes, 19! - Ways Trump and Republicans Are Plotting to Rig and Steal the Midterm Elections
bullets: Trump’s administration, led by Stephen Miller, has drafted legal memos and policy papers since early 2024 to condition federal aid—such as California wildfire relief—on states adopting restrictive voter‑ID rules and handing over voter rolls, effectively weaponizing aid to coerce Democratic states.

Republican allies are pursuing a multi‑pronged campaign—including gerrymandering, voter‑suppression bills, closing polling sites, voter purges, and threats of federal seizure of election records—to undermine registration, voting, tabulation, and certification ahead of the 2026 midterms.

Sources say senior Trump advisers planned these election‑rigging strategies months before his 2024 reelection, and the GOP now relies on a Supreme Court sympathetic to far‑right claims to secure legal advantages and enable potential federal takeovers of elections.

items.subject: Americans Live in the 'United States of Oligarchy' With Elon Musk at the Top
bullets: In June 2024 Elon Musk briefly became a trillionaire, a milestone the author argues proves America’s slide into oligarchy as Musk used his wealth to influence the 2024 Trump election and fund far‑right movements in the UK, Germany and elsewhere.

Musk’s post‑Trump ties birthed a self‑styled ‘Department of Government Efficiency’ that slashed federal programs, dismantled regulators like the FDA and FAA, and effectively let Musk regulate his own companies while securing lucrative contracts such as the $10 billion ‘Golden Dome’ missile‑shield project for SpaceX.

The piece contends Musk’s support for China’s regime—including praising its dictatorship and helping whitewash Uyghur genocide—shows how his wealth is built on aiding autocrats, reinforcing the claim that the United States now functions as an oligarchy dominated by a handful of billionaires.

items.subject: Israel Has Imprisoned a 16-Year-Old Palestinian-American Boy for Two Weeks
bullets: 16‑year‑old U.S. citizen Adam Wajeh Abdelfattah Karakrah was re‑detained by Israeli forces in the West Bank after his bail was paid, now held on a new rioting charge with detention extended past the planned release date
His family paid roughly $1,700 bail plus additional fees, reported threats and searches during a raid, and received only a vague embassy response that officials cannot intervene in legal matters
He joins at least 300 Palestinian minors and other Americans, such as 20‑year‑old Sama Safi, currently held in Israeli prisons amid broader accusations of rights abuses
